1.	Has the attention of the government been directed to the evidence given in the recent contempt case in Cornwall, Ontario, to the effect that a magazine distributor was required by the terms of his contract to take all magazines supplied by a certain company and in turn offer them all to vendors for sale, on penalty of forfeiting his contract of distributorship?
2.	Has the government referred this matter to the unfair trade practices commission for investigation under the Combines Investigation Act?
3.	If so, with what result to date?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
1.	The attention of the government has not been drawn to the evidence in question, but the director under the Combines Investigation Act noted it at the time.
2.	The government has not referred the matter to the director or the restrictive trade practices commission, which it is presumed is the body referred to in the question as the "unfair trade practices commission".
3.	See above. It will be remembered that the anti-combines legislation relates, generally speaking, to combines and monopolies in restraint of trade; to resale price maintenance; and to price discrimination. The director has in the past, as commissioner, given some attention to the magazine field and some years ago made preliminary inquiries into a similar complaint originating in a western city. He found that although the practice existed of requiring dealers to accept a complete "package" of magazines, they were entitled to return those that were unsold; and that opinion among dealers varied between those who favoured the system because it relieved them of the necessity of placing individual orders and those who objected to it because it required them to receive in the first instance and then take the trouble of returning unwanted lines. The commissioner came to the conclusion that, whatever the merits or demerits of the system, its nature was not such as to warrant formal investigation under the Combines Investigation Act and the matter is dealt with at some length in the commissioner's annual reports for 1951 and 1952 at pages 24 and 26, respectively. The director informs me that the newspaper report of Mr. Bryan's evidence indicated that the conditions he referred to arose out of a contract into which he had himself entered with the magazine distributor and that the incident did not, in the judgment of the director, in itself raise a case for investigation under the act.

speechtext:
In replying, Mr. Speaker, to questions asked by the hon. members for Duf-ferin-Simcoe, York West and Kent (Ont.) on March 18, I referred to a seasonal tariff which is applied when our own produce comes on the market. This tariff takes the
Inquiries of the Ministry form of specific rates of duty to replace the ad valorem rate ordinarily applicable on fresh fruits and vegetables.
Under the provisions of section 13 of the Customs Tariff, the Minister of National Revenue is authorized to order the application of these specific rates on importations from countries other than those entitled to the benefits of the British preferential tariff and for periods not to exceed those specified in the tariff items covering the products involved.
In ordering the application of these specific rates of duty, I am guided by recommendations made by the growers, through their organizations, and approval of such recommendations by officials of the Department of Agriculture who, through their inspectors in the field, have access to information regarding crop conditions and the availability to the trade of the Canadian grown product.
In the case of celery and onions, n.o.p., the specific rate of duty provided for in the tariff is one cent per pound and the maximum periods during which this rate may be applied in any fiscal year are 24 weeks and 40 weeks, respectively. During the remainder of the year the rate of duty on both of these products is ten per cent ad valorem.
During the present fiscal year, the specific rate was applied on celery imported into Ontario and Quebec for two periods totalling the full 24 weeks, that is to say June 5 to July 16, and September 24 to January 27, inclusive. The specific rate was applied on onions imported into these provinces on June 23 and will be cancelled effective the 30th of this month, when the 40 weeks' period will expire.
There is no information before us which would indicate the dumping of United States celery or onions on the Canadian market. However, if such were the case, the ordinary provisions of the dumping clause of the tariff would apply.

Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the
Opposition): Mr. Speaker, on different occasions during the present session questions have been asked of the government as to whether it was intended to continue the legislation now standing on the statute books under the name of the Emergency Powers Act. No answer has yet been given as to the intention of the government. Therefore it is appropriate, until we have information to the contrary, to assume that the government is contemplating the revival of legislation which has been discussed on a number of other occasions in the house. I submit it will be both helpful and appropriate if we consider the subject at this time, because if hon. members are prepared to indicate their opinion, that we should get back to government of the people, for the people, through their elected representatives in parliament, then subsequent time may be saved through the action of the government in acting in accordance with that expressed opinion.
TMr. Leboe.]
There are added reasons why the attention of the house should be drawn to the need for considering the grounds upon which sweeping powers of this kind have been taken by the government, with the support of a majority in parliament, and it is appropriate that everyone consider the tendencies indicated by some statements made within the last few weeks.
I know there are many hon. members who do not show any great interest when we discuss this subject, one which may be regarded as academic, but which in fact is anything but academic in its effect upon our parliamentary system and upon the future of government in Canada. There are those of us who believe that the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law mean more to us at this time than perhaps ever before in our history, since these principles were firmly established some three hundred years ago. We believe they are of vital and fundamental importance, because the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law more than anything else distinguish our parliamentary system from that authoritarian system against which the free peoples of the world are joining their strength at this time.
There is one principle of supreme importance if we are going to have government of the people, for the people, through their elected representatives in parliament; and that is the right of members and of the public to know the essential facts upon which decisions affecting the general welfare of our people or the economy of our country are made.
There is another principle of supreme importance which is at the root of the rule of law. That is the right of all people affected by any law to know in advance what the law is. We cannot expect everyone will know what every law is, in this period when there are so many laws. The principle however is at the very root of our freedom-the principle that the people shall have the right to know the law and, in turn, shall have the right to have an impartial and open trial, if it is alleged that they have broken any law. I know full well, without being reminded by any hon. member opposite, that this subject has been discussed in other sessions; it has not previously been discussed in this parliament. That is the reason I am bringing it forward today, so that not only in relation to the Emergency Powers Act, but in relation to other emergency measures, an opportunity may be afforded to hon. members to indicate their opinion in regard to the authority of parliament and the rule of law.
If I repeat today things that have been said before, I do so only because it is

necessary to repeat them through the failure of the government to act upon the arguments that have been presented to this house on earlier occasions. Added reason was given recently for considering very carefully what the attitude of the government is in regard to the rights of parliament and the people in connection with facts upon which public issues may be decided. I refer to a speech of the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) made on February 22 of this year. I intend to quote from that speech in view of the position under our constitution occupied by the Secretary of State. In quoting I am not relying merely upon newspaper reports but upon the text of the speech issued from his own office. Some of these statements bear careful examination in so far as they indicate the grov/ing belief of this government that it governs by its own authority, very largely, subject only to the subsequent approval of its actions by a majority of the members of this house. I now quote from the text of the speech by the Secretary of State:
It has frequently been stated that all documents in the possession of government departments deal with the public business, and that the public is entitled to know how its own business is conducted.
This is a very plausible doctrine, and one that is, superficially, quite attractive to most Canadians who believe in the democratic principle of government by the people. What is more natural than to say that if the people really control the government, the people are entitled to know about everything that goes on.
The Secretary of State regards this as a plausible doctrine and one with a natural appeal; but then he goes on to dispose of any thought that the government accepts that plausible doctrine, and he deals further with a motion before parliament in regard to papers and documents in the possession of the government, and he has this to say:
. . . this notion that parliament and the public are entitled to see every document in the possession of a government department is wrong, that it is contrary to the constitution; indeed it is subversive in the proper meaning of that word, by which I mean if it were accepted and applied it would upset the whole British concept of responsible parliamentary government.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we see the Secretary of State, the custodian of government documents, telling us that this plausible doctrine is not only not acceptable, but subversive. Those who might conceivably think that it was subversive of the parliamentary system to withhold facts are told on the contrary that it would be subversive if the principle were accepted that essential facts must be available.

On a question of privilege, if the hon. gentleman would not mind, would he use the word I used? I used the word "documents" not "facts".
Emergency Powers Act

This statement says quite clearly that it would be subversive if the essential facts were presented to the house which are contained in documents in the possession of the government and for which the Secretary of State is peculiarly responsible, in view of the statutory position he holds.
Will the hon. gentleman read the phrase where it says "essential facts".
I read it; it is correct. What I have read is the correct statement from the speech.
Read it, sir.

I have read it, Mr. Speaker. Hansard reports excellently and I am sure they have it correct. I shall go on with another quotation:
I suppose there is always some tendency for parliamentary oppositions to try to give the impression that under our system parliament is the government.
That is the end of the quotation, in case the Secretary of State gets in any way disturbed by any subsequent statement. Apparently in the mind of the Secretary of State, Mr. Speaker, there is the really very subversive thought that some of us might believe that government of the people for the people through their elected representatives should be a reality. Not at all; the government must be the sole authority, the sole custodian and the sole deciding body in this case, subject of course to the subsequent approval or otherwise, and, Mr. Speaker, there is a surprising consistency in the measure of approval given by the acknowledged majority of the supporters of this government.
Then I go on with a further quotation from the statement of the Secretary of State:
Parliament Is not the government and the government is not even a committee of the whole of parliament, though there is a certain sense in which the government can be regarded as a committee of its own supporters in parliament.
But I think it is much better to use the old-fashioned description of the relationship between government and parliament which was invented right here in Canada, and that is that the government is responsible to parliament.
Yes, in our belief the government is responsible to parliament, and we believe that parliament has the right to examine the manner in which the government is acting upon the basis of facts available to parliament, available to the elected representatives of the people who sit here in the House of Commons.
I quote again from this very interesting speech:
And once that decision is made, it is the duty of those who were entrusted by the voters with the

responsibility for government to carry on the government; and they should not share that responsibility with those who were not entrusted by the electors with the responsibility.
That is the end of the quotation, but it should have been the end of the speech. It should have been the end of any idea of this kind:
. . . they should not share that responsibility with those who were not entrusted by the electors with the responsibility.
There is a clear declaration of belief in the one party state.
No.

There is a clear declaration of belief in the idea that this is not a chamber where responsibility is jointly accepted throughout the whole house. Oh, I see some hon. members grimacing and shrugging their shoulders in surprise that this proposition should even be put forward.
This proposition is at the very root of our system. The government has the responsibility for initiating and presenting legislation to this house; and everyone in this house, under the basic principles of our parliamentary system, shares responsibility for what follows. May I add, Mr. Speaker, that those supporting the government are intended to inform themselves so that they may share that responsibility with some knowledge of the facts, as members of the opposition-or certainly some of them-seek to inform themselves.
Why do you not inform yourself first?

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to pay any attention to all the remarks I hear, but I intend to pay attention to the remark I just heard because it is illustrative of the attitude of those on the other side of the house. "Why do you not inform yourself first?" was the question that was just shouted to me from a point in the house where apparently the loud speakers do not work so well.

I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. I think 1 should tell the house that I was misinformed many times by the Leader of the Opposition while I was in the house in Ontario and I would not follow him for all the money in the world.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think that hon. members should not rise on questions of privilege which, of course, are not questions of privilege. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) now has the floor and should be allowed to make his remarks without interruption. If he is misquoting anyone or if he is making statements which, in the


opinion of certain members, are not in accordance with the facts, and if they are directly concerned with them, when the Leader of the Opposition is through they can rise and make the necessary corrections. But they should not do so in such a way as to interrupt the hon. member who has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of asking, as I am sure I have the right to do, for the withdrawal of the remarks that were just made. I am placing before the house an argument and the interjection which was just made is one that should be withdrawn if that request were made. But after all, I shall not make the request for withdrawal unless I think that the hon. member who has made the interjection is of sufficient importance in this house for me to make such a request.
Big man.

Mr. Speaker, I quite agree that this is not the first time I have heard the hon. member, and I know exactly the value to attach to his remarks now or on any other occasion.
Mr. Speaker, I referred to the statement made by the hon. member because it so aptly illustrated exactly the point I am seeking to make. He said "Why do you not inform yourself?". Mr. Speaker, that is what the opposition has been trying to do in many ways. I am pointing out that, in a speech made outside of the House of Commons but nevertheless one which expresses his opinion, the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) has clearly put before the people of this country his attitude toward parliament and the amount of information that should be available to members of parliament.
Mr. Speaker, this subject is one which does not arise here in Canada alone, and it is one for which this government alone need not accept responsibility. There has been a general tendency to move away from long-established principles of the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law, as a result of the effect of two world wars upon the administration of governments and parliaments similar to our own. This problem has been discussed in other parliaments similar to ours. This subject has been examined by great jurists as well as by members of this and other parliaments, and it has been examined by those with long experience in constitutional law. Mr. Speaker, the time has come-indeed it is long overdue-for the members of this house to assert a basic proposition which will change the trend and will start the members of parliament here

in Canada seeking some way, consistent with our increasingly complex society and economic system, that will nevertheless make it possible for parliament to have the essential facts in a way which will permit informed judgment by the members of parliament as well as by the people themselves with regard to subjects that are of public concern.
For that reason I hope that hon. members will not take to themselves the remarks that are made. In referring to any remarks that have already been made this afternoon, may I suggest to other members that they realize that this is a subject which is attracting great attention in every parliament within the commonwealth and that those in parliament and outside of it who have been studying this subject are seeking ways and means by which our complex economy and society may be efficiently informed while at the same time preserving those fundamental democratic principles of the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, this subject has been discussed before. It was discussed in this house by the former minister of justice and I should like to read words spoken by him in this house on November 12, 1945, because they indicate a steady trend by this same government. They indicate that this is no suddenly developed attitude which we find expressed in the words of the Secretary of State. These are the words of the then minister of justice, the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley, as reported at page 2020 of Hansard of November 12, 1945:
I should like to quote what the leader of the opposition said in this house on October 31, 1945, at page 1681 of Hansard:
". . . this House of Commons has the full and inalienable right to a disclosure of all actions of the executive. It has the right and the duty to review and pass upon all such actions. Except in some minor matters where the king's prerogative has not been abridged, the executive or cabinet acts properly only under authority delegated by this parliament. Thus, in order that we may be aware of the actions of the executive, I have placed this motion on the order paper."
Later in the same statement the hon. gentleman said this:
"I am determined to ensure, in so far as lies within my power, that Canada is governed by this House of Commons . . ."
Then the minister of justice had this to say about the words of the leader of the opposition at that time, to which he had referred and which he had quoted:
That statement is not historically or constitutionally correct. The house has not an inalienable right to the disclosure of all actions of the executive. Ministers may refuse to disclose matters if refusal to disclose is in the public interest and is so stated by the ministers.
Authority has been cited in support of that proposition. The house must accept the decision of a minister or withdraw confidence from the government, which it can do at any time. The authority 83276-2031
Emergency Powers Act of the government is not delegated by the House of Commons: the authority of the government is received from the crown. The membership of the government is not limited to members of the house. The true relationship of the House of Commons and the cabinet is a relationship of confidence. The essence of confidence is trust, not minute and detailed supervision of every act and every motive. Government cannot be carried on efficiently if every detail is subject to constant scrutiny.
There, Mr. Speaker, was a statement by the minister of justice at that time which did cause considerable surprise, as will be remembered by those who were interested in public affairs at that time, and who remember the comments which were made in the press and elsewhere about this. It is not easy to understand now how that statement was made without more serious challenge than was offered at that time. I want to read these words because I want to be sure they are correctly on record. I quote:
. . . the first step towards permanent recovery or reform in Canada must be the decisive repudiation by the Canadian electorate of the tendencies towards dictatorship manifested during the last five years, and an equally decisive repudiation of measures, by whatever party they may be advocated, which tend in the direction of Hitlerism, fascism or communism.
These words, Mr. Speaker, are clear. These words set forth in very definite and emphatic terms the attitude of those who do not believe that it is enough for the government to decide, and then at some subsequent time come back to the House of Commons and say, "Will you trust me? We have done this. The action has been taken and will you now vote in favour of what has been done?" These words, as I know members of the government are perfectly well aware, are the words of the man with whom the Secretary of State was so closely associated. I cannot help wondering at what point his thinking departed from the attitude of the man who spoke these words, because these strong words were the words of the late Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King dealing with the suggestion that the government had the right to withhold from parliament the facts upon which decisions should be made to resort to emergency measures. I would also like to quote something else said by the then prime minister at that time.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the hon. gentleman would permit a question? Would he give the date, place and circumstance in which these words were uttered, because their relevance to the situation is rather important?

Yes, of course. The relevance was very important. Mr. King, at that time, was leader of the opposition and he was expressing his views in regard to legislation

That was in what year?
In relation to what, sir?
In relation to parliament and the rights of parliament.
But in relation to what particular measure?

Mr. Speaker, I shall give the references. I am placing various statements on record. The statement I have just referred to was a statement by a man who was later prime minister of Canada, the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, who, during a period of opposition, supported certain principles in regard to the rights of parliament and supported them in words which will bear rereading by members of the Liberal party in this house today.

Perhaps the hon. member,
in order to make the rereading easier, would not mind giving the references. I suppose these remarks can be found in Hansard. Perhaps the hon. member would give the exact reference.

Certainly. But I am going to carry that statement further:
. . . there has been a further tendency of the gradual shifting over to irresponsible commissions, boards and delegates ... of a great deal of the business that should be carried on by the government itself . . . The country is being committed, directly and indirectly, to policies of which it has no knowledge, by persons who in no way owe responsibility to the people through their representatives in this house.
That last statement will be found in Hansard of March 1, 1920. The other one may be found in Hansard of 1935. I will give the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) the page number when I sit down.
Then on another occasion, to show the consistency of the views of the man who has put forward such a definite statement on this subject in years gone by, I would like to quote from another of the speeches by the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King:
The business of the country should be carried an in the open on the floor of this parliament in such a manner that the government will be obliged to take into their confidence not only members of parliament but the people of the country whose money they are voting to expend.
That statement may be found at page 4540 of Hansard dated June 30, 1920.
This is another quotation I would like to place on record:
It is impossible to imagine that the people of Canada will consent to pay the enormous sums


which they are being called upon to provide by way of taxation, ... or that they will sit silent under the government's refusal to give them any information as to how their money has been spent.
That statement will be found at pages 1292-93 of Hansard dated March 29, 1921.
And then, to bring us up to later years, I would also like to quote from another speech by the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King which will be found in Hansard of January 29, 1934:
The government has proceeded, in practically everything it has done, as if it were an executive wholly independent of the House of Commons rather than an executive which derives its powers from and is responsible to the House of Commons.
Compare that statement, Mr. Speaker, with the statement made by Mr. J. L. Ilsley. Here is a proposition that is consistent with the long tradition of parliament, stated by a man who has generally been accorded respect for his knowledge of parliament by members of the Liberal party. I would like to repeat these words because they are words which emphasize how far this government has departed from the proposition it has put forward itself on many occasions. I repeat these words:
The government has proceeded, in practically everything it has done, as if it were an executive wholly independent of the House of Commons rather than an executive which derives its powers from and is responsible to the House of Commons.
Then, on January 21, 1935, the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King had this to say, as found at page 32 of Hansard:
The whole spirit of the British system of government is that government is carried on, not by arbitrary powers secured by a mechanical majority, but by the consent of the governed as known . . .
You will notice in that quotation that the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King used a term which perhaps overcame some of the objection that has been registered with relation to other words used to describe a majority which votes with fascinating regularity in one particular way. He spoke of a mechanical majority. There is no record of objection having been taken to that word at that time by anyone in the house. I should like to quote further words of the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King from the same speech. He said:
I have said that one of the supreme efforts of this administration-
That of course was not a Liberal administration because it was not a Liberal administration at that time.
-has been stealthily to alienate the authority and control of parliament, to take power into its own hands and away from parliament with respect to many important affairs of the nation.

Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does my hon. friend agree that the words he has been quoting were fitting words for the right hon. gentleman to have applied?

Mr. Speaker, that is exactly the type of comment that I have come to expect from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Gar-son) . I was quoting the words of a man who has been recognized and acclaimed on other occasions by the minister who has just interrupted me as an authority on parliamentary procedure. I have pointed out on other occasions that, no matter what disagreement there may have been with regard to the many details of the things that were done, I did believe that the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King understood the principles of parliament, and it would be a very good thing for the present Minister of Justice to remember them when the time comes for him to draft any further legislation bearing on subjects of this kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Now try answering the question.

I was just about to point out, when I was interrupted by the Minister of Justice, that the quotations I have placed on record are quotations which indicate that this is not a subject with regard to which members of only one party have been expressing concern. This is a subject about which members of all parties in this house and members of the different parties in the House of Commons at Westminster, in Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and elsewhere throughout the commonwealth, have been expressing great concern in recent years.
I wish it were possible to examine this question as one of common concern. I wish it were possible to examine it with the idea that we might now start back toward some system that would have full regard for the vast and infinite variety of detailed subjects that must be dealt with but would at the same time make it possible to give hon. members of this house, as the representatives of the people, an opportunity to obtain essential information which would qualify them to pass judgment with knowledge of the facts. That, after all, was what the Right Hon. Mackenzie King was emphasizing. He wanted the facts to be known. He wanted the important details put before the house. He recognized that every single piece of information could not be brought before the house but he did want the business of the country carried on in parliament and not behind closed doors. That is the view we have been
Emergency Powers Act expressing. That is the hope with which we place this subject once again before members of the house.
I referred to the speech made outside the house by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill). An interpretation of his opinions certainly shows that he has gone several steps beyond the position taken by the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley and that the position he takes is one which would never have been tolerated in silence by the man who was prime minister of Canada for so long and with whom he was closely associated. We have asked for assurance that under these changed conditions the government would reverse its course. A clear indication of that would be a statement by the government that it definitely will not seek the support of the majority in the house to continue the Emergency Powers Act on the statute books of Canada.
A consideration of this legislation is *appropriate at this time in so far as the intent behind the introduction of such an act may be examined. Now is the time to avoid unnecessary subsequent debate with regard to either this or any other emergency legislation. That can be done if hon. members will only make it clear that they wish no continuance of emergency legislation of that kind in a period when we are as close to normal conditions as any of us are likely to be for many long years to come.
Last year the Emergency Powers Act was renewed. It is still on the statute books and unless renewed again will expire on May 31 of this year. The terms of that act involve an attitude consistent with the view expressed by the Secretary of State, consistent with the view expressed some years ago by the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley, but not consistent with the view expressed by the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King and not consistent with the view expressed by many people of different parties who today are seeking some new method to give real parliamentary responsibility to the members elected by the people and to restore the rule of law instead of the rule of dictate such as we have at this time.
It is not enough to say that no harm has been done. Great harm was done last year to the principles of parliament by something that was done under that act. Without reviewing the orders in council passed in 1951 and 1952, as well as in 1953, under the Emergency Powers Act, may I say that the most outrageous example of abuse of emergency powers occurred on Monday, April 20, last year. What happened then should be in the minds of the members of this house when we consider today the

Emergency Powers Act attitude of the government towards the extension of any emergency measures which give to the government the power to legislate behind closed doors.
Those who were sitting in this house at that time will recall that the house met at eleven o'clock on the morning of April 20 last year. It was dealing with amendments to the shipping act, and that was the place where anything affecting shipping, and the rights of ship owners or others, could have been discussed, with knowledge of what was being done, by members of this parliament. It was very significant that while that act was under discussion that morning the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), under whose department the administration of acts of this kind must come, absented himself from the House of Commons during that discussion. In his absence the amendments were approved, and in due course the bill was given third reading in order that it could be passed on for consideration in the other place.
After the house had spent only a few minutes in the transaction of some other business, to the very great surprise of hon. members in this house, the Minister of Transport made his appearance in the house just before the one o'clock adjournment. He proceeded to ask for consent to revert to motions, and permission was given by unanimous consent. He thereupon tabled two copies, in English and in French, of order in council P.C. 1953-604, passed three days before that, on Friday, April 17, under the provisions of the Emergency Powers Act. This order in council, which had been passed three days before and had the effect of law, was of very great interest to many ship owners in this country and was presented here in that way. Earlier the same morning we had been discussing an act to which these changes could very properly have been amendments.
There was no reason whatever for the provisions of that order in council, because they could have been enacted as part of the provisions of the Canada Shipping Act. I just heard an interjection to the effect that is not so. It is so, Mr. Speaker. It is true we were told three days later that this was part of a general agreement of some kind, but there was no general agreement. I hope the time will never come when there will be general agreement that this government has the right to enter into any understanding with any other government which will deny to this parliament information to which it is entitled. It most certainly could have been made an amendment to the Canada Shipping Act, or failing that it could have been a separate piece of legislation introduced by


the minister who had been piloting the Canada Shipping Act through the house. Members who were sitting here could have passed upon those amendments in the ordinary way. Instead of that, an order in council was passed behind closed doors, given the effect of law, and in that way many people had their position substantially affected without the members of parliament having an opportunity to deal with the subject.
Let us go back to the time when this act was before the house on February 20, 1951. At that time the Emergency Powers Act was being considered, and the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) was explaining why this act was being presented. I quote what he said on that occasion from page 497 of Hansard for that date:
The question may be asked, what is the nature of the emergency we are facing? In the opinion of the government, it is as defined in the following language in the speech from the throne:
"The increased menace in the Far East reinforces the mounting evidence that communist imperialism is determined to dominate the world by force or the fear of force, and that the only hope of maintaining peace with freedom lies in the rapid increase of the combined strength of the free nations."
That was the reason we were given in 1951, Mr. Speaker. No one suggests today that we have passed the time when we need to be careful to maintain our strength against the threat of communist aggression. However, we have passed from the immediate emergency state which arose following the attack in Korea, and have entered a stage of longterm duration when we hope that, as a result of the mounting strength of the partnership of free nations, peace may in fact be preserved. There is a very real hope that the full horror of the kind of war that would result from the use of the new weapons which have been accumulated to meet the possibility of that threat may in themselves offer a hope of peace in the years ahead.
If it should happen, this will not be the first time in history, by any manner of means, that great military powers available for military action have, in fact, assured peace over a long term of years. I believe that the hope of every one of us here is that the money that is being spent for defence today will have that effect. Nevertheless, we have been told by the government here, we have been told by statesmen associated with us in this common effort, that this is going to be a long period of sustained effort. If we are to have peace, it will only be the result of carrying on for a long time under conditions which require from us very definite military preparations, and which also offer hope to us of peace through the might of the defence that is being built up.

This is a subject, Mr. Speaker, in which all have a common interest. I did not quote for the record here today the words of a former prime minister merely for the purpose of seeking to embarrass any minister of the present government or to establish the inconsistency of views that have been expressed. I did so to demonstrate to this house how far we have strayed from the position that was commonly accepted by most members of this house.
When I am asked whether I agree with words that were spoken at that time, may I say that it is most interesting to have anyone offer the suggestion today that the very limited powers in the hands of the government in the early part of 1935 bore even the slightest similarity to the immense emergency powers held by this government today. And yet, in relation even to those very limited powers, we found the then leader of the Liberal party using these strong terms:
The first step towards permanent recovery or reform in Canada must be the decisive repudiation by the Canadian electorate of the tendencies towards dictatorship manifested during the last five years, and an equally decisive repudiation of measures, by whatever party they may be advocated which tend in the direction of Hitlerism, fascism or communism.
Mr. Speaker, there were those who laughed at Mr. King when he spoke those words.
Oh no.

Oh yes, there were. When an hon. member says, "Oh no", I say there were people who laughed at Mr. King at that time. And there are people who laugh today at the suggestion that there is any danger in a trend of this kind.
No, I am not going to suggest for one moment that the words of Mr. King as to the possibility of Hitlerism, fascism, or communism are appropriate. And I do not think those words were appropriate then. But I do think the statement he was making in regard to the principles of parliament-in spite of the giggling of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) at the moment-I think those were important principles.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I believe the rules of the house require my hon. friend, as a member, to accept the word of another member as to what he was doing. Mr. Speaker, I can only express my great regret at the pain which produced the grimace on the face of the Minister of Justice at that moment.
Mr. Speaker, I believe this is an opportunity for members in the house to express an opinion in regard to this subject, without testing the position of the government in relation to any legislation before the house. It is an opportunity for members to make their comments respecting emergency legislation of this kind. It is an opportunity for members in the house to give to the government a clear indication that the trend should be back toward greater responsibility on the part of parliament, and that there should also be a greater recognition of the principle of the rule of law.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, so that this subject may be dealt with by hon. members, through the opportunity provided in this instance, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green):
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted, and the following substituted therefor:
"this house desires to record its opinion that the powers granted to the governor in council under the Emergency Powers Act are repugnant to responsible parliamentary government."

Mr. Speaker, I was just about to say that I think we have listened to a speech this afternoon which does serve a useful purpose, because it brings before us a problem of government and parliament.
Last year we opposed the legislation now under discussion on the ground that the government had not used it as we anticipated it would have been used. The Emergency Powers Act was first placed on the statute books in 1951. In that year we understood that the legislation would be used in the interests of the Canadian people to prevent further inflation, to protect the people from the rising costs of living, and the like. This was not done. Consequently, when the measure came before the house last year we opposed it on those grounds.
I can see some circumstances under which legislation of this description is necessary;
3204	HOUSE OF
Emergency Powers Act but I do not believe that that necessity exists at the present time. I do not know-because one does not have the research facilities one would like to have-how many times this legislation has been used since last May, when the house approved its extension. I doubt very much whether it has been used to any extent. And if it has not, then that is the first argument why it should not be extended or continued at the present time.
What the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) has said about the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law is certainly something of which we should take heed, wherever we may sit in the House of Commons. May I say particularly at this time that at least one public man in this country, in the person of the premier of Quebec, is challenging the supremacy of parliament; and, indeed, if reports can be believed, is challenging the rule of law, when he says that a federal act passed in relation to deduction of income tax for federal purposes will not be fulfilled by the government of the province of Quebec.
I say that every member in the house, no matter where he sits, should regard himself as a guardian of the supremacy of parliament and a defender of the rule of law, no matter whom it may affect, whether it be an individual, a corporation or a government.
As I listened to the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon, that was the thought that flashed into my mind. At the beginning of his speech he said that the supremacy of this parliament and the rule of law are of fundamental importance to this country, and, indeed, at this time, to the world. I would like to remark that we should keep that constantly in mind as we discuss measures of this description, and other problems, that face the country today.
We shall support the motion at this time because we believe that, since the Emergency Powers Act has not been used in the manner in which it should have been used, and perhaps has scarcely been used at all, its continuance is not consistent with responsible parliamentary government. I am one who believes in parliamentary institutions and the parliamentary system. I believe as a matter of fact that for the self-government of man- and I use that in the sense of including both men and women-no better plan has yet been devised by man. And I want to see the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law properly maintained. But I think the government will have to make a case for the retention of this legislation. I am not going to say very much today, but I will say, as we did last year, that we shall indicate our opposition to any proposed extension by 

voting for the amendment that has been introduced by the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon.
During the war years perhaps this parliament did grant to the government many prerogatives and rights which ordinarily should have been exercised by this house. We were forced to do so under those circumstances. I suppose there will be times during peace and in war when governments of all stripes will ask for powers that go beyond what is normally granted in a legislative body of this description. I say, under certain emergencies powers of this sort must be granted, but I do not believe that the situation exists at this time which warrants this parliament, under the circumstances, considering, if the proposal is made-it has not been made yet-extension of the powers that we gave to the government several years ago, and the more limited powers which we extended last May.
I do not wish to speak at any further length, but merely to express the point of view that I have just expressed and to say that I hope that every hon. member, wherever he sits, will heed the plea of the Leader of the Opposition for the maintenance of the supremacy of this parliament and of the rule of law throughout the whole of this country.

Mr. Speaker, it would seem unfortunate that such an important question as has been injected into parliament this afternoon should not have been known a bit in advance, because some of us would like to have made better preparation in detail so as to be able to cite specific cases to the point, and make of this debate what it really should be.
I look upon this matter as of the utmost importance, and it is because I do look at it as of the utmost importance that I said what I did, namely, it is too bad we did not have some indication that it might be raised this afternoon. However, the Leader of the Opposition has raised it, and I for one would not like to see the occasion pass without registering briefly views which I have with respect to the very important principles of the rule of law and the supremacy of parliament, which are the subjects of discussion.
For a good many years thinking men and women all over the world have been concerned about insidious attacks that have been made on these two important principles of democracy, the isupremacy of parliament and the rule of law. No less a person than Lord Hewart of Bury, a member of the House of Lords, began away back in 1927 to register his fears through various publications. He wrote a book known as "The New

Despotism" and he brought it up to date in 1949, when the second edition was published. I should like to indicate just briefly from Lord Hewart's book one or two of the important views which he held, and by doing so I hope to be able to show hon. members that as far back as 1927 Lord Hewart of Bury saw what was happening in parliament. He observed this gradual but steady decline in the rule of law and in the supremacy of parliament and the gradual increase in the use of executive order by order in council to govern the country, and to do it without the knowledge of the representatives of the people.
I am not going to quote at any length, Mr. Speaker, but I do want to use just a few of the statements made by Lord Hewart of Bury to illustrate the importance of this matter. He said:
A little inquiry will serve to show that there is now, and tor some years past has been, a persistent influence at work which, whatever the motives or the intentions that support it may be thought to be, undoubtedly has the effect of placing a large and increasing field of departmental authority and activity beyond the reach ot the ordinary law.
This has been done very largely through two methods, as far as I can understand: First, through the manner in which our various acts of parliament or laws are drafted by draftsmen who put into them certain clauses making it possible for the minister or the government, the executive council, to make regulations and even to go so far as to change the nature of the law and its provisions by regulations. That has been known. It has been done right here in this parliament over the years, and the process has gone on almost unimpeded for a number of years.
Lord Hewart went further and said this:
The citizens of a state may indeed believe or boast that, at a given moment, they enjoy, or at any rate possess, a system of representative institutions, and that the ordinary law of the land, interpreted and administered by the regular courts, is comprehensive enough and strong enough for all its proper purposes. But their belief will stand in need of revision if, in truth and in fact, an organized and diligent minority, equipped with convenient drafts, and employing after a fashion part of the machinery of representative institutions, is steadily increasing the range and the power of departmental authority and withdrawing its operations more and more from the jurisdiction of the courts.
In my experience in parliament we have never had a wide-open debate on this important matter. It would be very much in the interest of the country to have such a debate, where we could be better prepared for it, although the subject has been introduced here this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition and it will serve a real
Emergency Powers Act purpose in alerting our people, not only in this house but across the country, to what is going on. Yet the full value cannot possibly be realized unless we are more thoroughly prepared for it than we are this afternoon. Lord Hewart pointed out in his thesis that to the average lawmaker, the average proponent of democracy, the continental system of administrative law was repugnant. I believe that is right; it is to me, although I must admit right out, Mr. Speaker, that the continental system of administrative law is at least a system, and it does provide for courts and law and hearings and adjudications and all that sort of thing, with which it attempts to preserve for the people their rights and liberties. Then, Lord Hewart went on to point out that although the continental system of administrative law is repugnant to the average proponent of democracy, yet it has some superiority over the kind of rule of law into which we have declined in these days.
The rule of lawlessness.

Yes, the rule of lawlessness; it might be wise to say that, as the hon. member for Kamloops remarks. This insidious process -and I call it insidious because anything that saps the strength of the parliamentary institutions is insidious-has been going on for enough years so that the people of the country should be aware; but I say to you that the people of the country can hardly be aware of the process and its insidious nature unless they can get the facts. There is only one way in which they can get the facts and that is if the government of the day, which is supposed to be a democratic government in this country, will make those facts available to the members of parliament, the press and to the public generally. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that that procedure has not been considered by the Liberal government, as long as I have been in the House of Commons, to be a responsibility of theirs. In fact, there have been times when the members of the opposition have sought for information and have been denied it. Why, I have never yet been able to learn.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: May 1 ask the hon. member a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I know very well the book to which my hon. friend refers, and I am sure that in that book there is nothing that deals with this particular aspect of the problem. Lord Hewart was referring to excessive administrative powers given to administrative tribunals, where there was no right of supervision by the courts, and so on.

Emergency Powers Act I am sure that on that particular issue he did not express himself as my hon. friend implies he did.
Oh, yes. I am sure the minister has not read the book recently or he would not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Oh, yes; I have.

The fact is that Lord Hewart dealt with the same thing we are dealing with here today. He definitely deplores the way in which parliaments have been denied their responsibility. I will see that the minister gets the book when I am finished so that he can read up on it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: 1 shall be grateful if my hon. friend will show us right now where Lord Hewart says that the kind of thing complained about by the Leader of the Opposition today is contrary to the well-known practice in the United Kingdom parliament, let alone in the other commonwealth parliaments.

All right, Mr. Speaker. I do not mind doing so. If the minister will tolerate a few more quotations, I think I can give it to him. I am having to pick these quotations more or less at random as I have not had time to prepare for this debate as I should like to have done. At page 16 of his book he simply says:
It is not merely that in this instance parliament is being out-manoeuvred, or that in that instance the courts have been defied. It is that the whole scheme of self-government is being undermined, and that, too, in a way which no self-respecting people, if they were aware of the facts, would for a moment tolerate.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Yes. He was talking about administrative tribunals and royal commissions.

No. He was talking about exactly the same thing we are talking about, namely the rule of law and the supremacy of parliament, just exactly the same things that were introduced in the speech made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew). Lord Hewart goes on to say:
Much toil, and not a little blood, have been spent in bringing slowly into being a polity wherein the people make their laws and independent judges administer them. If that edifice is to be overthrown, let the overthrow be accomplished openly. Never let it be said that liberty and justice, having with difficulty been won, were suffered to be abstracted or impaired in a fit of absence of mind.
The paradox which is in course of being accomplished is, indeed, rather elaborate. Writers on the constitution have for a long time taught that its two leading features are the sovereignty of parliament and the rule of law. To tamper with either of them was, it might be thought, a sufficiently serious undertaking. But how far more attractive to the ingenious and adventurous mind to employ the one to defeat the other, and to establish a despotism on the ruins of both!

What else could he be talking about but the rule of law and the supremacy of parliament? That is quite plain to be seen.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Yes. That is what he is talking about.

Speaking of some kings of old, he goes on to say this:
In those days the method was to defy parliament-and it failed. In these days the method is to cajole, to coerce and to use parliament-and it is strangely successful.
To use parliament. What for? To set up, Mr. Speaker, a despotism or a narrow type of oligarchy for the purpose of governing a country which is supposed to be democratic. Then Lord Hewart goes on and gives a lot more things which I do not believe I need to quote. I am going to help my friend the minister by giving him some of the recommendations which Lord Hewart made and which I think he will see apply to the very case in point. At page 147, in a chapter entitled "What is to be done?" he says:
If it be asked where the remedy is to be found for the mischief which is here deplored, the answer is not difficult. Is it too much to hope, in the first place, that the worst of the offending sections in acts of parliament-
I direct attention to the words "acts of parliament".
-may be repealed or amended? And, in the second place, is it not comparatively easy to prevent similar sections from being enacted in future? To this end what is necessary is simply a particular state of public opinion, and in order that that state of public opinion may be brought into existence what is necessary is simply a knowledge of the facts. At present, it is tolerably safe to suppose, only a small part of the electorate knows what has been and is being done, while it is a still smaller part that has any real appreciation of the meaning and effect of the statutory provisions which offer at once the occasion and the instrument of despotic power. Two methods at least may be adopted, easily and immediately, by those who desire to discourage the new despotism. One is to form in each house of parliament a committee,-
And I put this forward as a suggestion to the Liberal side of the house particularly because they are the ones that can do something about it.
-not too large, whose sole task It should be to examine every bill, as it is introduced, for the purpose of observing whether and in what respects its provisions may have the effect of increasing the power of bureaucracy, and whether and by what contrivance that power is to be made irresponsible.
If that is not a suggestion along the line that my hon. friend-
