So does Mr. Manning, I am quite certain.
He has said so many times.

The situation is simply this. The government has not brought forward the Emergency Powers Act for discussion today; not at all. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) injected this discussion into the proceedings of the house today.
I just wanted to make those observations because I want to use them to support the stand we have always taken in connection with these emergency powers. Let me make it abundantly clear once more. I recognize the fact that there are times when the government needs unusual powers. When the need is clearly expressed, when that need has been demonstrated, when the government comes to this parliament and asks for those powers, and when I am convinced that they need them to meet a situation which exists,
Emergency Powers Act I will not withhold my consent for whatever it is worth in this house. That is the position we have taken in years gone by and that is the position we take today. On the other hand, when the government year after year asks for an extension of the Emergency Powers Act and then does not use the powers that are given, thereby demonstrating that there has never been any real need for them, I for one do not intend to agree at any time to the extension of those powers unless once more it has been demonstrated, by logical argument, that the government needs them.
I do not know what the government is going to do about these emergency powers this year, but I do want to submit my view that we should have in this house a watchdog committee of the type suggested by Lord Hewart, which committee could make a very careful scrutiny of all legislation in order to see that bills are properly framed and do not contain the kind of clauses which will curtail or filch from parliament its right to control the government of the country, which is a responsibility placed upon parliament under a system of parliamentary government.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Secretary of Slate):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not rising to speak in reply to the motion made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew). I am not competent to do so, because the question is one of government policy which, as the Leader of the Opposition, and every other hon. member of this house, is well aware, has not yet been determined. The hon. gentleman was told this only last week by the right hon. gentleman who was then acting prime minister. I imagine those of us who believe it is important to maintain parliamentary traditions wonder in passing whether this attempt to anticipate a debate which might come before the house later on is altogether in accord with the usual parliamentary traditions. I do not think it is, though I do not believe it is out of order. But I shall not argue that point.
The only reason I am taking up any of the time of the house, Mr. Speaker, is that my name has been mentioned and the remarks I made in a rather modest afterdinner speech made in another place seem to have caught the eye of the Leader of the Opposition. I confess I am rather flattered that he should have read that speech. I am even more flattered that he should have considered it sufficiently important to be made the excuse or the occasion for a debate, because I stated in that speech-though the hon. gentleman did not see fit to read it- something to the effect that all politicians live on advertising and on having their names
3208	HOUSE OF
Emergency Powers Act before the public. I recognize this and I give my thanks to the Leader of the Opposition for bringing my name thus briefly before the house. But I am afraid my agreement with the Leader of the Opposition ends just there.
Well, sit down.

No. I am now going on to
disagree with the Leader of the Opposition, which I believe is the proper function of an hon. member in debate.
I suppose there are some hon. members opposite of the mechanical minority-if I may use the word of Mr. Mackenzie King of which I was reminded by the hon. gentleman-who think that anyone who speaks in this house should not disagree with the Leader of the Opposition. Well, I do not agree with the Leader of the Opposition. I do not agree with the fundamental statement he made. He quoted from a speech made by Mr. Ilsley some years ago in this house, and also from a speech I made some days ago in another place, and referred to certain things which had been done by this government inside and outside of this house, and before I was a member of it, which he said indicated a tendency towards a one-party state. I do not agree with that at all.
I said in the speech from which the hon. gentleman quoted that I supposed there was always some tendency for parliamentary oppositions to try to give the impression that under our system parliament is the government, and then I went on to say:
Parliament is not the government and the government is not even a committee of the whole of parliament, though there is a certain sense in which the government can be regarded as a committee of its own supporters in parliament.
That is where the hon. gentleman said I should have stopped. But I am not going to stop there. I am going to say this to the hon. gentleman. I do not believe in, I do not want to see, and I am totally opposed to a one-party state. I believe an opposition which does not agree with the government should not support it. When the hon. gentleman says there is a joint responsibility in this parliament which should be accepted by all hon. members on both sides of the house for what the government is doing, I would then ask who is advocating the one-party state? Is it the people on the opposite side who say they want to share the responsibility for what the government is doing? Or is it those of us in this house who say that as long as the electorate and members of parliament give us their confidence it is our responsibility exclusively and we have got to take the blame? If the opposition can persuade the electorate they can do


better then they will be on these treasury benches. But if I cross over to the other side of the house I shall not wish to share their responsibility.
That, I believe, is a true parliamentary system, and this notion that in some mysterious way the opposition has a share in the responsibility for carrying on government is not. The opposition has a duty and a very important duty which, it seems, they sometimes forget. They have a duty to harass the government and to point out mistakes in government policy. They have a duty to give a coherent, responsible program to the public so that the public has a chance of electing an alternative government. I question very much if they have made much effort to do that since 1935.
I am not talking about emergency powers, and I do not intend to do so except to make one observation later on. I am talking about the reference made by the Leader of the Opposition to the speech I made. I believe the difficulty is, and it is a difficulty which is inherent in Conservatism, that it is impossible for a real Conservative to believe that the public could want anyone else to carry on the government. That is why, after an election, they always want to reverse the verdict of the electorate and to crawl into office even though the public has indicated they are really not wanted.
I believe the public has indicated that fairly decisively, particularly in the last two elections. All I was talking about in this speech of mine, which has been the occasion though not the real reason for this debate, was the question of procedure in parliament in regard to motions for the production of papers, and addresses to the crown for papers. There has been considerable discussion about this on the other side of the house and statements made have been, if I may use my own words, rather plausible, and rather misleading to people outside the house. I tried to give to a number of gentlemen and a few ladies, who did me the honour of asking me to speak, an explanation of what the ancient parliamentary practice was in regard to these things. The Leader of the Opposition, if I took his words down correctly, said there was a tendency to move away from these old practices.
I said I would not agree with the Leader of the Opposition. I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, but I have to agree with him in this instance. I believe there has been a tendency to move away from these old practices-on the part of the opposition. To illustrate my point I would like to read a passage on this question of motions for papers from Bourinot, who was a clerk of this house some time ago and

who, I do not think, can be accused of any of the latter twentieth century innovations we have had here.
What page?

I have the fourth edition, published in 1916, and in this copy it is on page 249. It reads:
Occasions may arise when the government will feel constrained to refuse certain papers on the ground that their production would be inconvenient or injurious to the public interests. A high authority writes on this point:
"Considerations of public policy, and a due regard to the interests of the state, occasionally demand that information sought for by members of the legislature should be withheld, at the discretion and upon the general responsibility of ministers. This principle is systematically recognized in all parliamentary transactions; were it otherwise, it would be impossible to carry on the government with safety and honour."
Consequently, there are frequent cases in which the ministers refuse information, especially at some stage of an investigation or negotiation; and in such instances the house will always acquiesce when sufficient reasons are given for the refusal.

Exactly, when sufficient reasons
are given.

I continue:
On this account, members will sometimes consent to withdraw their motions; or in case only a part of the information sought for can be brought down, they will agree to such alterations as the minister may show to be advisable . . . sometimes the government may be obliged to withhold all information at the time, or they may be able to put the house in possession of only a part of the correspondence. If the government objects to the production of documents on the ground that they are of a confidential nature, it is not usual to insist on their being furnished, except under peculiar or imperative circumstances, on the ground that it would be wholly without precedent to produce them.
I could read a lot more to the same effect. This is the ancient practice. That is all I was describing in this modest little effort of mine. I was not attempting to suggest that the executive should take the place of parliament or anything else. But I did give reasons why some of these documents should be refused, and in view of some of the other things that have been said in this chamber this afternoon, much as I dislike the practice of quoting one's self I am going to do so right now, and I will make the quotations as short as I can. In the speech referred to, I had just been quoting the privy councillor's oath with which the hon. gentleman who leads the opposition is, to my knowledge, familiar because I administered it to him myself, and it gave me great pleasure to do so. I then was in another capacity.
I had referred to the privy councillor's oath which I do not need to remind the hon.
Emergency Powers Act gentleman obliges ministers not to disclose what takes place in Her Majesty's council. I said:
Now the main reason why deliberations of the council are and should be kept secret is that privy councillors, like other human beings, sometimes have minds of their own and occasionally have differences of opinion about the course of action to be taken by the government. But the government itself can only take one course of action at a time-
I think I should have said "can take only one course of action".
-and since all ministers are responsible for every action taken by the government and are in duty bound to support the action of the government-
Or to resign.
-our kind of government would be impossible if differences between them which have to be resolved were not kept secret.
In view of certain experiences that some other countries have had, I think the salutary nature of our system will be appreciated. But I gave another reason which perhaps some hon. members would think I might be a little more touchy about than most members in the house. I said that on many occasions documents which are asked for in these motions are documents which pass between officials and ministers. I think it is known to every hon. member that, for quite a long time before I came into the house, I was a bureaucrat, and for most of that time I was very well treated as a bureaucrat.
Hear, hear.
Yes, I agree with the hon. member.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: But deservedly so.

But towards the end of my career as a bureaucrat I suffered something which some other public servants in this country, perhaps for less reason, have also suffered. An attempt was made to go behind the minister who was responsible for my conduct and to bring me into a controversy when I could not reply. I am not complaining about that in my own case at all. As a matter of fact I have taken means whereby I can now defend myself to the best of my abilities against any kind of attacks. But most civil servants-and I hope this will continue to be true-do not aspire to political careers. They do not want to have political careers and they should not be put in the position where they either have to have a political career if they want to defend themselves or they have to stop giving honest, courageous and sometimes disagreeable advice.
Under our system civil servants are not entitled to explain or defend themselves, their

Emergency Powers Act opinions or their advice in public, and they should not be allowed to do so. Because they are divorced from politics and because it is essential to the proper working of our system that they should continue to be divorced from politics, it is absolutely essential that the documents which they prepare for the advice of their ministers, setting out the arguments pro and con, stating the advantages of one course and the advantages of another, and sometimes tendering advice that some ministers do not accept-because that does happen -should not be made public. To protect civil servants, to protect the very system under which we operate, the rule has been established that parliament is not entitled to see documents passing between public servants and ministers. Such documents are, in the language of parliament, privileged.
That is all I was talking about in this attack on parliamentary institutions that I am supposed to have made. That is absolutely the only point I was making. I think it is the duty of a government to protect these documents, to protect the people who prepare them, and to do so is not denying to parliament any essential facts whatsoever. The facts that a government is obliged to produce here, that it has a duty to produce here, and that this government in my experience has always been willing to produce, are facts, and not opinions, not arguments as to alternative possibilities and that sort of thing, on which ministers, either individually or collectively, have to make up their minds.
The facts to which parliament is entitled are the facts on which the government reaches a conclusion. It is the duty of the minister to give them. It is his duty to give them in his own words and on his own responsibility, and if he does not do a good job of it the opposition should make his life miserable until he does. But they should not sneak around by the back door, if that is not unparliamentary, sir, and try to burgle the minister's briefcase and to do it by motions for papers in parliament. That was my only point and that is my only point.
In my opinion the sooner we get back to the ancient practices and the ancient ways and the sooner hon. gentlemen opposite return to the old fashioned practice of attacking ministers and of making ministers answer for their departments, instead of trying to get behind them to attack defenceless civil servants, the sooner we will have good debates in parliament, and the sooner we will have greater respect for parliament in the country. Now I, sir, am not going to give any lecture-

Perhaps the minister would agree to tell the house at what point any

hon. member this afternoon made any suggestion that could be interpreted in the words he has just used?

I do not think I said any hon. member did, Mr. Speaker. As I recall it, I was describing what I had said at a dinner at the Chateau Laurier. I said that there were times when motions were put down here that would have that kind of effect. I did not say in the debate this afternoon any hon. member had said anything of that sort. At least, I do not think I did. If I did, I did not mean to do so. If I did, I withdraw it.
I was saying that it does not seem to me that the fact the government feels it has a duty to resist motions for the production of privileged documents is interfering with any of the rights of parliament or any of the rights of the opposition. I feel it is upholding the ancient parliamentary practices, upholding our way of doing things and making our kind of responsible government workable. That is my whole point. If any hon. member opposite wishes to read the whole of what I said, without just taking a fragment here or there-not that I object in any way to the way in which the hon. member used the quotation he made from my remarks, I only objected to the occasion when I thought he departed from my text and put in the word "facts". I have carefully gone over what I said and I found no occasion where I said anything about the denial of facts. I do not think it will be found anywhere in my remarks.
Will the hon. minister permit a question? We have not had that speech identified. Where was it delivered and when?
I would be delighted to do so. I apologize to the hon. member for not having sent him a copy.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: We thought you made it in the Senate. You kept talking about "another place".
Not in the Senate yet, anyway.

The hon. member will have to pardon my inexperience in using terms of that kind. It is described here as "cabinet government and freedom of information." You know, they always ask you to give a title and I thought that one up. The title is not very bright or original. It was a speech delivered to the semi-annual meeting of the Canadian Weekly Newspapers Association at the Chateau Laurier hotel in Ottawa, on February 22 of this year.

In referring to the Emergency Powers Act, the Leader of the Opposition quoted from Mr. Mackenzie King. He gave one or two quotations, which he said he was not giving to embarrass anyone on this side of the house. I can assure the hon. member they did not embarrass me, and for two reasons. They did not embarrass me because they were taken from a period long before I had ever met Mr. King. They did not embarrass me because I agree fully with what was in them. I particularly noted, and took down so I would have them right, certain words he quoted from one of Mr. King's speeches. Mr. King said that the executive had derived its power from, and is responsible to, the House of Commons. That is precisely what I was saying here. It is precisely what Mr. Ilsley said. Mr. Ilsley said the power was not delegated by the House of Commons. Everybody knows it is not delegated; that is not the mechanical way it is done, if I may use the word "mechanical" here.
He said the power was derived from the House of Commons. We who sit on the treasury benches here are nothing-
That is right.

-the moment we cease to have a majority of this house to support us on any question. Therefore, we derive our power from this house, and we acknowledge that. It is true that there are certain people in this house, quite a large number, who were elected to support us and keep us here. There were a certain number of members elected not to support us. We do not derive our power from those who were elected not to support us. Surely that is a self-evident fact.
What really makes this whole question rather difficult is the fact that, when motions are moved by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) or the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles)-though the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is usually more in order-asking for papers which they know quite well no government would give and which they themselves certainly would not give if they were in office or they would not stay in office very long, the newspapers frequently say the government refused information to the house when those motions are voted down. The twenty people who sit on the treasury bench cannot vote them down. It requires the majority of the house. The government is not refusing information to the house. We would not dare.
Emergency Powers Act
If the house, by a majority vote, asks for information we must either give the information or we get out of office. It is just as simple as that. That is what responsible government really means. It does not mean giving some information that some hon. member opposite would like to have in order to show there was a difference of opinion between me and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). I may say that never happens, but it might happen. It might even be reflected in a document or a letter I would write to him. If it did happen, I would not blame the hon. member for trying to get that correspondence. I mean, it is part of the game.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Who would be right then?

They are not right, however, when they say that if we will not give it to them we are defying parliament or destroying the rights of parliament, because we are not. That is my whole point.
I feel I can perhaps reinforce this a little by reading one paragraph of this speech that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) did not read. When I have read that, I think that is the only other quotation I shall inflict on the house. I recognize that I was talking to newspapermen, whose business it is to get information in any honourable way they can, and what I was saying was not very palatable to them. I tried to explain the case as well as I could, and then I went on to say:
I am sure that every true newspaperman is. by instinct, against secrecy. He makes his living by uncovering news and reporting all the facts to the public. No one would question the right of newspapers-
At least I would not, perhaps I was going too far when I said "no one". In fact, I am sure I was going too far because I seem to remember the Leader of the Opposition did question this right in the case of the radio on one occasion.
No one would question the right of newspapers to report any differences of opinion between cabinet ministers they are able to discover for themselves, or to publish reports or even speculation about the advice ministers have received from their officials or from experts they have retained, subject always to the ordinary laws of libel.
It is one thing for the press to discover these things for themselves, by any means they have at their disposal which they can exercise without falling foul of the law, and it is quite another thing to say it is the duty of the government to provide this parliament with such information. That is the point, and the whole point. If I can sum it up, parliament has the right to know what the government's decisions are, and it has the

Emergency Powers Act right to have reasonable justification lor those decisions and the best case the government can make for them from the government benches, but it has not the right to have all the papers which we have used in making up our minds. That is the essence of it; because those are not public documents at all.
Now, I do not think there is anything more I can usefully add to this subject. However there is one other point upon which I think, as an historian, I would like to make a slight correction. The Leader of the Opposition, in one of his quotations from Mr. Mackenzie King-and I did not take a note of it, I am sorry to say-when Mr. Bennett was in office, contrasted his statement with the situation prevailing under the Emergency Powers Act.
Now, as I recollect it, Mr. King's objection to that legislation of Mr. Bennett was that large sums of money were made available, without any specific appropriation, in a time of peace. That was the point. Appropriating money is a function of parliament. It is true that during the war there were huge general appropriations under wartime conditions; but I do not think this government has asked for any appropriation of that kind in peacetime. And under the Emergency Powers Act we have specifically excluded the power to appropriate money without a specific reference to parliament. In other words, I do not think the quotation was relevant to the kind of circumstances we are discussing in this motion.

Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) has spent most of his time this afternoon trying to explain and to justify the foolish speech he made outside the house some weeks ago. He has said very little about the Emergency Powers Act; and so, if one is to be in order in following him, there is very little one can say about the hon. member's speech. I would like to make one remark, however, and it is this, that I think after he has had a little more experience as a cabinet minister and has been told a few things by senior cabinet ministers, he will not be so brash about making foolish statements outside the house, and will not come to the house and try to convince the rest of us that, after all, they were not foolish.
The amendment before the house is as follows:
this house desires to record its opinion that the powers granted to the governor in council under the Emergency Powers Act are repugnant to responsible parliamentary government.
It is worth while for us first to look at the attitude of members of the government with regard to this question. I refer for


example to the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) on March 12, just ten days ago. He was asked this question by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) when the orders of the day were called:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Acting Prime Minister. With the approach of the Easter recess, is he in a position to say whether or not it is the intention of the government to allow the Emergency Powers Act to lapse, or will legislation be introduced to continue it?
One would have thought that the Acting Prime Minister would have treated the subject with great seriousness, and that he and other members of the cabinet would have given a great deal of time to consideration of this question, which is so vital to the parliamentary life of Canada. But here was the minister's answer:
Mr. Speaker, no decision on that point has been taken as yet. It will depend upon events between now and the end of the session.
That was the very offhand answer given at that time by the right hon. gentleman, showing how little weight he placed on this particular question.
And then today we have another evidence of the attitude of the government, in the very fact that instead of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) of this country, or the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) leading off for the government in answer to the amendment, we have the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill), the most junior member of the cabinet-or very close to it-getting up and leading off for the government, making a speech which ignored the Emergency Powers Act, and trying to show what a great fellow he is, himself.

May I repeat that these actions show more clearly than words could do that the present government places very little importance on this question of the Emergency Powers Act, and very little importance on parliament- because it is the strength and power of parliament that is involved in this question. They show further that the government has lost all sense of the values in the democratic system of government.
Further, Mr. Speaker, I point out that during only four years of the life of this Liberal regime have we had a free parliament in Canada; and that was from October, 1935, to September, 1939 when the War Measures Act was brought into force. Ever since the fall of 1939, for a period now of almost fifteen years, there has been no truly free parliament in this nation. Parliament has not been supreme.
A year ago we had a debate with respect to the extension for a further year of the Emergency Powers Act. It was a hard-fought debate, all the opposition parties uniting to attack the government's proposal that the act be extended. As a result of that debate a column was written in the Vancouver Sun by the present member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott). I shall read two or three paragraphs from that column, because I think it shows very clearly what a Liberal thought a year ago about the Emergency Powers Act-and goodness knows there is far less cause for continuing it this year than there was last.
This is what the hon. member for Vancouver South had to say-and I shall be very interested to see how he votes on this amendment. The column is headed "Sees Liberal Mistake". It is dated February 25, 1953, and is as follows:
It seems to me that the Liberals at Ottawa are clearly in the wrong, and the Conservatives, C.C.F. and Social Credit clearly in the right about extension of the Emergency Powers Act. Under the regular constitution of Canada the government of Canada has all the powers that it needs to deal with any conceivable emergency. Moreover, in this age of air travel, it is possible to assemble parliament on 48 hours' notice or even less.
Why, then, ask parliament for what amounts to a blank cheque to by-pass parliament even when parliament is sitting?
Emergency Powers Act
It would be wrong at any time for a government to ask for the extension of the Emergency Powers Act, unless there was some clear and unanswerable case for such a request. But it seems doubly bad for a Liberal government to do so,-
Mr. Philpott did not know his Liberals then as well as he knows them now. I continue:
-for the most fundamental principle upon which historic Liberalism stands is precisely the supremacy of parliament.
When young Mackenzie King came into power in Canada after an energetic campaign in 1920 and 1921 when, day after day, he aroused the people of this land to the dangers of rule by order in council.
The principle he championed was right then-and it is right now.
And then he goes on:
A bad principle is a bad principle-and this is a very bad principle. A bad precedent is a bad precedent-and this is a very bad precedent.
On November 26 I asked, in my speech on the debate in reply to the speech from the throne, that this Emergency Powers Act be repealed. If I remember correctly, no attempt was made to answer that suggestion, and of course no move was taken by the government. We are now in a position where, according to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the government does not know, the cabinet does not know, what they are going to do about the question.
It is worth while today, Mr. Speaker, to go back and have a look at this Emergency Powers Act. Of course we have on the statute books the War Measures Act, which could be brought in by proclamation even though war is only apprehended and not actually a fact. The War Measures Act was used during the war years, and I have heard no one quarrel with such action. In the postwar years modified measures were brought into effect. The War Measures Act was put back in cold storage, where it remains at the present time, and different acts were enacted to replace it. There was the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act, and then this Emergency Powers Act, which was passed on March 21, 1951. It is very interesting to analyse this act and see what it provides. In the first place it reads as follows:
Whereas an international emergency exists that threatens the security of Canada;
In other words, it declares an emergency. That is the first point I wish to deal with in connection with the act. The second point is this: It is based on preparations for defence. For example, the second recital reads as follows:
And whereas it is essential that emergency powers be conferred to enable measures to be taken as urgently required from time tc time to carry out adequate defence preparations,-

There are the words I mentioned a moment ago. Then, the recital goes on:
-to regulate the economy of Canada to meet the needs of defence-
There is another reference to defence. The paragraph continues:

Therefore the second feature of the act that I wish to deal with in a minute is that it is based on defence preparations. The third feature is in the third recital which reads as follows:

And these are the words I emphasize:
-present efforts to avert war are continuing and, moreover, it is not desirable that the wide powers conferred by that act to interfere with the fundamental liberties of the individual should now be brought into operation.
The third feature I am emphasizing today is in these words:
So long as present efforts to avert war are continuing.
The fourth feature is the powers actually set out in the act.
First of all, to go back to the declaration of an emergency; as Your Honour knows, the very fact that parliament passes an act declaring an emergency widens the jurisdiction of this parliament. The result is that if a person attempts to attack an act which was passed by this parliament he may be met with the defence that parliament has declared an emergency. That is particularly true of an attempt by one of the provinces to attack the jurisdiction of this parliament to pass an act. Counsel for the defence will probably be met in court with the argument by counsel for the dominion that this Emergency Powers Act declares an emergency, and therefore the act in question is intra vires. That declaration of emergency gives the dominion power it should not have under present conditions; it is an inaccurate description of the situation at the present time, and I go further and suggest it is a deceptive description of conditions at the present time; the dominion is not entitled to have this extended jurisdiction which is gained by declaring that there is an emergency.
With respect to the second feature of the act, defence preparations, I challenge the Prime Minister or any minister of this government to indicate how this Emergency


Powers Act is needed for defence preparations. For the production of defence materials we have the Defence Production Act. When it was passed in 1951 I asked the Prime Minister whether or not that act gave the government all the powers it would require if a third world war were in existence. The question and answer are to be found on page 909 of Hansard of March 5, 1951, as follows:
The Prime Minister has said that this bill as presented contains all the powers that would be required in the event of a third world war.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I would not want to promise the house that if we ran up against something where the courts said this was not good enough we would not come back to parliament; if we thought it should be done, we would ask parliament to authorize it; but I think the law officers have drawn this in language that should be sufficient to cover all the enabling powers apt to be required.
Therefore for the purpose of defence production, even though we were in a third world war, nothing more would be needed than what is on the statute books in the form of the Defence Production Act.
Then, a day or two ago this house passed the Export and Import Permits Act, which again I suggest is an act which would be sufficiently strong, even though we were in a war. In any event, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, with this Export and Import Permits Act in his hands, has all the powers he requires. He does not need to get any further under the Emergency Powers Act.
The third feature of the act, namely, that it is passed to be effective so long as present efforts to avert war are continuing, leads me to say this. The act was passed in March, 1951. The fighting in Korea ended on July 27, 1953. The men in our forces, even though they are serving in Korea, are now being treated as though they were serving in a peacetime army. They are no longer entitled to the benefits that were available for men who served during the fighting in Korea. Our whole force now is on a peacetime basis. And, Mr. Speaker, if the emergency powers are needed now I wish the Prime Minister would explain when they would not be needed.
If this Emergency Powers Act is to be continued, then it is only too evident that emergency powers are from now on to be the regular thing in Canada, during the whole time that there continues in effect this present policy of remaining strong so that an aggressor will be dissuaded from commencing a war. That policy will probably be in effect for the lifetime of most of the members in this house today. Is parliament to be fettered with an Emergency Powers Act

under present conditions? If so, it is a rather bleak outlook for parliamentary government in Canada.
To come to the powers granted by the Emergency Powers Act, we find that they are contained in section 2 thereof. They are very wide. The section reads as follows:
The governor in council may do and authorize such acts and things, and make from time to time such orders and regulations, as he may by reason of the existing international emergency deem necessary or advisable for the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada:	and for
greater certainty, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms, it is hereby declared that the powers of the governor in council shall extend to all matters coming within the classes of subjects hereinafter enumerated, that is to say:
Then we have a list of these powers specifically covered by the act.
(a)	control and suppression of maps, plans and photographs;
(b)	control of communications and means of communication:
(c)	control of the harbours, ports and territorial waters of Canada and the movements of vessels:
(d)	transportation by land, air or water and the control of the transport of persons and things;-
In other words, all transportation across this country.
(e)	trading, exportation, importation, production and manufacture;-
I ask hon. members how you could have wider power than that.
-and (f) imposition and recovery, in connection with any scheme of control, of fees or charges payable to the Receiver General of Canada or into any fund or account established by order or regulation for the purposes of the scheme of control.
Then the section goes on to provide as follows:
All orders and regulations made under or pursuant to authority conferred under this act have the force of law while this act is in force.
That means, Mr. Speaker, that under this act legislation can be made by the cabinet over in the east block, behind closed doors, and can be enacted even while parliament is sitting. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) smiles; and he is the right man to smile because, just about eleven months ago he walked into this house and tabled an order in council that under this act had been passed over in the east block with the doors shut and the blinds drawn.
That is what I was smiling at.
I hope they had the lights on.

That order in council was
passed without any opportunity for debate in this house, without any opportunity for the press of Canada to report a debate to the public and without any opportunity for

Even with respect to this order in council which was tabled by the Minister of Transport and known as the "control of trade by sea for mainland China and North Korea", P.C. 1953-604, there has been in the intervening eleven months no attempt to place that law in statute form, even though this session it could have been brought in as an amendment to the Canada Shipping Act, and something of that kind should be done. When the government did that, of course they were challenged. The following day I moved an amendment to the motion to go into supply and challenged that action. Here was the reaction of one of the senior ministers of the government who was in the house at that time. I refer to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. If we have overstepped our powers, I make no apology for having done so.
That was the attitude then. In effect, these powers are a club in the hands of the government held over parliament, over the Canadian people and over the provinces.
As to the question of the rights of parliament, Mr. Speaker, clearly this Emergency Powers Act forces parliament into a secondary position subservient to the cabinet. It should be fundamental in Canada that parliament is supreme. After all, parliament is the people governing through their representatives under your direction, Mr. Speaker. That should be the foundation of parliamentary government in this country. Parliament should be supreme, debating laws openly, with the right to deal with them in the various stages as they go through this house and then as they go through the Senate, so that the people are able to know the problems, the remedies that are proposed, the objections made to the legislation and, perhaps most important of all, the penalties that are imposed by those laws.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that this Emergency Powers Act should be repealed. Certainly it should not be extended beyond May 31. Any orders in council that are in existence under the Emergency Powers Act could be changed into statutory form by having them passed in the ordinary way by the house. If when

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have just heard a very interesting speech on the merits of the Emergency Powers Act, which is not before the house at this time. We have before us a motion to go into committee of supply, to which there has been moved an amendment which reads as follows:
this house desires to record its opinion that the powers granted to the governor in council under the Emergency Powers Act are repugnant to responsible parliamentary government.
It occurs to me, Mr. Speaker, that that is quite an unusual amendment to make on a motion to go into supply. It is an attempt to anticipate something which may or may not happen. The Emergency Powers Act, as everyone knows, is an act of temporary duration which will expire on the 31st of May, unless there is an attempt made to have legislation passed by this parliament to extend it for a further period. If that is done it should be within the powers of parliament at that time to decide whether the act should be extended.
This is an attempt to have that decision made at the present time so that there can be no bill introduced or dealt with by the house to extend the act. That does not seem to me to be required at this time. If we intended to do as the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) seemed to believe Would be the right thing to do, namely, to set up the kind of committee which Lord Hewart recommended in his book, from which the hon. member read some very interesting quotations, there might be some point in dealing with it now. But this can have no other effect than to reflect upon what parliament did during another session, because it is a declaration by this house that what was done in this house by another parliament, and which received royal assent, was something that was "repugnant to responsible parliamentary government".
I do not know just exactly what is meant by the words "responsible parliamentary government". I assume the word "government" is used in its widest sense, to include everything that has to be done for the peace, order, and good government of the state through our parliamentary institutions. This amendment in effect proposes that this house declare that what was done is repugnant to responsible parliamentary government. I think that course is objectionable under standing order 41, and that which has been sanctioned by usage both in England and

Canada, namely, in effect, that an hon. member while speaking must not reflect on past acts and proceedings of this house.
There is a way of dealing with legislation which has been passed and which hon. members feel should not have been passed, that is by the introduction of a bill to repeal it, but here is an indirect move designed, I imagine, to put it beyond the powers of this house to deal with that kind of legislation were it introduced during this session.
I believe we are all very happy that in the course of the last few months there has been no occasion when we required the use of these powers, and I believe we will all be very happy if they never have to be used. It may be that between now and the time when it would be necessary to introduce legislation for an extension there will be happenings that will make it quite apparent to everybody that the powers granted under this Emergency Powers Act would not be required, and that they would be merely a standby to ensure that we would be in a position to meet events unlikely to occur. But parliament in its wisdom-and that is how we must regard the result of parliamentary action- decided last session that it was going to make these powers available up to the 31st of May, 1954, and not beyond that date unless the matter were again raised in the meantime.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) seems surprised that the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Howe) said that we had not yet decided whether we would ask parliament to extend that act. Why should there be anything surprising about that? It is something that does not have to be dealt with and does not require to be dealt with until the end of May. The world situation during these troubled years is subject to frequent changes. Why should we make any decision? No one would be happier than members of the government if the situation became such that parliament did not have to be asked to extend the Emergency Powers Act.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister a question. Does the Prime Minister believe there is any need for the act under present conditions?

Emergency Powers Act such that it was a proper discharge of our responsibility to have the act available. Now it is available and will be available up to the end of May. No one disputes the supremacy of parliament, no one disputes the rule of law, but oppositions always take a different view from that of those who happen to have the responsibility of government at the time as to what is impairment of the rights of parliament. Strong language has been used today. If it ever became necessary for us to sit on the other side of the house I would not be at all surprised if there might be some occasions when we would use just as strong language as is now used by the opposition about these impairments of the rights of parliament. But nevertheless it is a fact in which I think the Canadian parliament and the Canadian people can glory that others than Canadians recognize that there is no country in the world where the practices of constitutional parliamentary institutions are better than they are in Canada, and that in spite of the fact that there have been these constant charges that those who are exercising the responsibility of government are becoming dictators or are resorting to methods that connote Hitlerism or fascism or communism.

I even heard favourable comparisons being made with respect to democratic practices in the northern half of the North American continent with some of the things which many of our friends to the south of us themselves deplore in the administration of their own system.
That being the situation, there is no application to parliament at this time to pronounce itself in favour of extension of the Emergency Powers Act. There is no necessity of making a formal decision at this time, and in spite of the charge that it may be docility on the part of members who were elected to support this government, I invite them to vote against the amendment because if they were to vote for it they would be doing something not required at this time, something which may never be required, namely, to make up their minds whether or not there are sufficient reasons to justify the extension of the life of that act.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister permit a question before he concludes with that point? I ask him to appreciate that I am seeking information. Can he tell us whether the order in council which we sometimes refer to as the secret order in council, and which was passed under the authority of the Emergency Powers Act, is still in existence?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That being the case, what would happen to it if the Emergency Powers A.ct were allowed to lapse on the 31st of May?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It would disappear; it would lapse. It may be that it will be possible to allow it to lapse and that there will be other provisions under which what this order in council wards against can be taken care of.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: If any such other provisions are adopted in connection with that secret order in council, would there be a report to parliament that another basis had been found for it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There would not be
another order in council required. It may be that in dealing with the Criminal Code and in dealing with the Official Secrets Act there will be sufficient safeguards against that which is warded against by the secret order in council to make an order in council unnecessary. It would not be something that would have to be specially dealt with by order in council having the effect of law.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In other words, it might die without-
It would be a safeguard existing through the operation of the statute itself.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In other words the order in council itself-
No.
Will you permit me? I should like to hear the hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The order in council might die without our ever having known what it was about.

Yes, and I do not think that would be an infringement upon the supremacy of parliament or upon the rule of law. It was something which we felt was a necessary precaution, and if we can find legislation adopted by parliament sufficiently specific to ward against the danger which it was attempted to ward against by the order in council, then the order in council would appear unnecessary. It would certainly expire if the Emergency Powers Act itself expired because there is no other foundation for it to rest upon but the authority given by parliament to do so. If that authority lapses, it will lapse at the same time.
The situation is changing. An international conference is to be held with respect to which some hopes are entertained that it may bring about some easing of existing tensions. I refer to the Geneva conference to commence, I think, on the 26th of April. That is well before the 31st of May. On the other hand situations might arise out of the discussions of the Geneva conference which would appear to be quite otherwise. Although the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra said that the fighting ceased on the 27th of July, it must not be forgotten that that is only a ceasefire.

The troops were put on a
peacetime basis.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
They were put on a peacetime basis, and I think the hon. member hopes, as I hope, that they will never be put on any other basis. But it is only a cease-fire. That has to be followed by something. I saw the very strong lines that have been provided in Korea, and I said the other day that the best intelligence our people had was that on neither side were offensives being prepared. But it would not be reasonable to anticipate that armies are going to stand there in these impregnable lines facing each other forever. There is going to be some solution some day to the stalemate represented by these two defence lines.
These are matters which will be dealt with in due course here. There is a provision in standing orders, Mr. Speaker, which does

not directly apply, but it does indicate the principle which should be applied when government business is being dealt with. It appertains to the government to decide in what order and at what time it will be dealt with.
This is an effort by the opposition to have something that is government business decided weeks and weeks in advance of the time when the government itself feels that it should be decided. If this house adopted the motion, then there is the principle that the same question cannot be again submitted at the same session. Citation 304 of Beau-chesne's second edition reads:
It is a wholesome restraint upon members to prevent them from reviving a debate already concluded; and it would be little use in preventing the same question from being offered twice in the same session if, without being offered, its merits might be discussed again and again.
If a bill to extend the emergency powers were offered, either Your Honour would rule that we could not answer the arguments made against that kind of bill this afternoon by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) or Your Honour would rule that the same question could be debated twice during the same session.
There is a general rule that deals with amendments that can be made to the motion to go into supply, and it says in part:
. . . provided that the discussion and the amendment, if one is moved, shall not relate to any decision of the house during the current session, nor to any item of the estimates, nor to any resolution to be proposed to the committee of ways and means, nor to any matter placed on or whereof notice has been given in the order paper.
There is an indication that that principle should apply to this motion. There was no notice required on the order paper to make it abundantly clear that the Emergency Powers Act could not live beyond May 31, 1954, unless legislation were introduced to carry that out. I think it would be in accord with the general principles of the rules that no decision should be taken on this matter today. Should the general rules be too general to allow Your Honour to rule on this amendment, I think that the supporters of the government should wait to express their opinion as to whether the Emergency Powers Act should be extended until the government comes to the house with the reasons why it should be extended.
The government will not come to the house unless it has reason to feel it would not be discharging its responsibilities to the Canadian public without the act. I invite our followers in the house to withhold their judgment upon the sufficiency or insufficiency
Emergency Powers Act of the reasons, if reasons are brought forward, until those reasons are brought forward.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: With regard to the citations the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has read to the house I wanted to say that, as 1 heard the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) speaking about existing legislation on the motion to go into supply, I thought that perhaps it was not the type of grievance that is customarily put before the house on the motion to go into supply.
Will you hear argument?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am not going to make a ruling at the moment, I just want to deal with the procedure. I looked at the citations having to do with these amendments that are moved on the motion to go into supply. If hon. members look at citation 345 and then at citation 467 of Beauchesne's third edition, they will find that wide scope is given to amendments moved to the motion to go into supply.
At one point citation 467 says that amendments can be moved and it shall be permissible-I am not quoting verbatim-to discuss any public matter within the powers of the federal parliament. Then it says:
. . . provided that the discussion and the amendment, if one is moved, shall not relate to any decision of the house during the current session, nor to any item of the estimates, nor to any resolution to be proposed to the committee of ways and means, nor to any matter placed on or whereof notice has been given in the order paper.
I could not see how the matter being discussed at the moment was one which fell within the restrictions of citation 467 or 345. The Prime Minister has drawn my attention to a citation in Beauchesne's second edition, which in the third edition is citation 246. It says:
Besides the prohibitions contained in standing order 41, it has been sanctioned by usage both in England and in Canada, that a member, while speaking, must not:
(k) reflect upon the past acts and proceedings of the house;
The last few words of standing order 41 read:
No member may reflect upon any vote of the house, except for the purpose of moving that such vote be rescinded.
Now, if hon. members look at citation 246(k), they will see that this language is probably a summary of citation 244, which says:
A member may not speak against or reflect upon any determination of the house, unless he intends to conclude with a motion for rescinding it.
In my opinion the "past acts" referred to in citation 246(k) mean past acts in the same

Emergency Powers Act session. I do not think we ought to rule out of order a declaration of principle embodied in an amendment to a motion to go into supply, because of the wide scope offered for such amendments; I do not think we ought to say that, because of this citation, members cannot criticize acts passed in previous sessions. The whole spirit of our rules pertaining to bills or motions which are not to be offered twice refers to the same session.
I might perhaps refer hon. members to May's Parliamentary Practice, the twelfth edition, at page 267, where it deals with the same question. It deals with this citation, which in Beauchesne's is the same in substance, and comes from May or Bourinot. It goes on to say how difficult it is for a member who wants to discuss the past action of a parliament in the same session to move a motion to rescind it because there has to be a new question put before the house. It is said that the house has even resorted to prorogation in order to rescind a decision made in the same session.
I submit that if hon. members look at the authorities they will see that a session of parliament is assembled by the summons of Her Majesty and continues until prorogation. In my opinion the limitation is to a debate taking place twice in the same session. I think that paragraph (k) of citation 246 refers to a debate in the same session.
Now, I was trying to see if there were any words in the amendment which perhaps might be offensive. I looked up the definition of the word "repugnant" and I find in the Oxford dictionary, which is on the table, that the word is defined as meaning "contradictory, incompatible with, refractory, resisting, distasteful". If we were to decide that "distasteful" is the proper definition of the word repugnant, then I should think hon. members would want to modify the expression. But if it means incompatible with responsible parliamentary government, which I think is the meaning, while in the ordinary sense it is considered a bit strong, I believe, upon looking at the definition, that we should not have such thin skins as to say that the word should be prohibited or, under our rules, eliminated.
I do not want to make a ruling at this moment. I have given my thoughts in the matter-perhaps given them too quickly- but, at first sight, looking over the authorities, that is my reaction. I promise hon. members that I will study the point further, and if I find any reason for changing my mind I shall communicate it to the house.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I understand this afternoon when I was on the front lawn of the parliament buildings trying [Mr. Speaker.!

to count how many daffodils are pushing their way up through the snow, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) referred to a newspaper article I wrote about a year ago. I do not know whether that was the first best or the second best article I wrote on that particular subject a year ago, but I am sure the hon. member would not want to leave with the house any misapprehension.
I wrote two articles about a year ago concerning the Emergency Powers Act.
Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to interrupt the hon. member but-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) has just come into the house, and is rising on what is called a question of privilege. Hon. members generally do that either immediately after or while a speech is being made. In this instance I understand the hon. member for Vancouver South was not in the house.
He may do one of two things: If he knows what has been said he may explain the position briefly, without adding anything other than that required to make his position clear; or he may wait until he has an opportunity to take part in the debate, at which time he would be entitled to discuss fully the point brought before the house. But I do not think that at this time he can add anything that would not be considered necessary to making his position clear.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, I shall take my two minutes now. The addendum to the article which I understand the hon. member read this afternoon was to the effect that we needed the Emergency Powers Act last year, during the period when we had no parliament to call in an emergency session. And of course I still stand by that position. So, in answer to my hon. friend's query, he does not need to be in any doubt about how I shall vote tonight. I shall vote with the government. If for any reason the emergency powers were to be prolonged beyond that period, without justification, then naturally I would vote against the government. But tonight I shall vote against the opposition because it seems to me this is a vexatious move.

Mr. Speaker, I am very glad of the ruling you gave because, so far as I can make out, the real difficulty is that the opposition is coming in too close and is making suggestions which are somewhat embarrassing to the government. Perhaps unintentionally the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) gave me a good deal of hope this afternoon that actually what we are asking is going to happen. And also he gave me a certain feeling of satisfaction

that although we did not succeed a year ago in having this legislation turned back, nevertheless we may have succeeded better than we knew in not having it used. Because we now find that the government saw fit not to use it at all during the year just past. To that extent I think we may be entitled to congratulate ourselves.
When we examine further into the use of this statute, and look back to the orders in council which were passed, the strange thing is that a great many of them seem to have very little to do with the actual reasons for which we understood the statute was passed. On that point I shall have something more to say after the dinner recess.
At the moment however I should like to go back to a year ago and to say a word or two about what the Prime Minister has said as to the inappropriateness of the resolution, inappropriate because the government has not yet declared its mind. I noticed carefully what he said to members of his own party.
I would ask him to go back to a year ago, and consider what happened. At that time, for the first time-I think almost for the first time-we felt that there was throughout the country some indication that people were becoming interested in this question of undue government power. The hon. member who has just spoken on a question of privilege, and who is going to vote with the government tonight, was one who did come out and express views in which he questioned seriously what was going on.
This year, with the legislation having still some months to run, we have been bold enough to seek to arouse public opinion and to influence the government, while there is still time. I suppose if we had been good little boys we would have waited, and would have done nothing until the government reached its decision. Then, in theory, we would have been able to put forward our arguments and if those arguments had been good enough, the government would have adopted them. I am a modest man, Mr. Speaker, and I, frankly, do not ever expect to be able to make arguments good enough so that, when the government has brought in legislation and has shown its hand, it will be persuaded by those arguments to change its procedure. Neither do I expect to live long enough to see members on the government side rise up and smite the government. That is something which, in the best of all possible worlds, might happen, but I do not believe it will happen in this world, or in this parliament.

We will go on winning all the debates but losing all the votes.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

Emergency Powers Act AFTER RECESS
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. During the recess I examined the point that was brought up prior to six o'clock and I want immediately to refer hon. members again to citation 246, paragraph (k), Beauchesne's third edition, which reads:
Besides the prohibitions contained in standing order 41, it has been sanctioned by usage both in England and in Canada, that a member, while speaking, must not:
(k) reflect upon the past acts and proceedings of the house.
I gave it as my opinion that past acts did not refer to any other act but those which had been previously passed in the same session. It appears from reading the various authorities on the subject that it may not be right that it refers only to the acts passed in the same session but also to previous acts passed in other sessions. I should like hon. members to listen to a paragraph which is found on page 194 under the chapter "Rules of Debate" in a book published by Sir Gilbert Campion in 1950. There they will find paragraph 5 which reads:
This rule applies also to insulting language against a statute as the work of parliament.
This question and others to follow are all linked to the language contained in our standing order 41, which has to do with offensive and disrespectful language. The exact meaning of the word "act" in all these citations is somewhat difficult to establish.
In May's fifteenth edition at page 436 you find under the heading "Words against Parliament, or either House" a subparagraph entitled "Against a statute" and the following:
Disrespectful or abusive mention of a statute would seem to be partly open to the same objections as improper language applied to parliament itself; for it imputes discredit to the legislature which passed it, End has a tendency to bring the law into contempt; though the necessity of the repeal of a law justifies, as an argument for that course, its condemnation in debate. A statement that the enactment of a law may justify an appeal to force is not within the cognizance of the chair.
I am now going back in the years because, as hon. members know, our standing order 41 dates back to 1867, and we have inherited it from similar standing orders which existed under previous parliaments in Canada and in England. In Bourinot's fourth edition, which was published in 1916, I find the following: "Rules for the preservation of order.-Parliamentary and Unparliamentary Expressions in Debate," and at page 361:
(x) or to reflect upon, argue against or in any manner call in question, the past acts and proceedings of the house.

Emergency Powers Act
If "past acts" mean a statute which is in force and has been adopted by a previous parliament at a previous session, Bourinot would certainly not like to see us discuss at this moment the powers in the Emergency Powers Act because he says:
Or to reflect upon, argue against or in any manner call in question, the past acts and proceedings of the house.
In Bourinot's third edition, which was published in 1903, I find at page 482:
Or to reflect upon, argue against or in any manner call in question, the past acts and proceedings of the house.
Then in Cushing, which was published in 1874, I find at page 672, citation 1740, which reads as follows:
It is irregular to reflect upon, argue against, or in any manner call in question, in debate, the past acts or proceedings of the house, on the obvious ground, that, besides tending to revive discussion upon questions which have already been once decided, such reflections are uncourteous to the house, and irregular in principle, inasmuch as the member is himself included in and bound by a vote agreed to by a majority: and it seems that reflecting upon or questioning the acts of the "majority" is equivalent to reflecting upon the house.
Hon. members would judge that in this citation he is referring to a vote previously made in the same session. I am at a loss to decide exactly what is meant by "past acts". It looks as if generally the latter part of our standing order 41 is to the effect that if one wants to criticize an existing statute he must propose a motion to rescind a decision which has been previously made. It looks as if that is the sense of it.
What I should like to submit to the attention of hon. members at this time is the following: If one wants to argue against a statute, what is the objection to his proposing a bill to repeal that statute? Why does he have to take recourse to an amendment to the motion to go into supply? I looked at precedents. By the way, it certainly does not involve any expenditure of money to propose a repeal of a statute. I find that in 1936 the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) proposed a bill to repeal an act to establish an economic council, which had been passed by a previous parliament. It appears at page 436 of Hansard, volume I. The hon. member asked for leave to introduce a bill, which was agreed to. Hon. members will find at page 578 that the motion was agreed to and the bill read a third time and passed.
The question before us at the moment is: Should we consider it a grievance and delay the examination of supply to move as an amendment to that motion what is tantamount to a repeal of an act? It seems to me that


this amendment, to be scrupulously in order, should be modified to read: "That the administration of the powers granted to the governor in council under the Emergency Powers Act is repugnant to responsible parliamentary government." I should like to submit this because I think we all want to respect the traditional rules of order in debate. I should like to submit to hon. members that in whatever we do we should always follow the best course, and the best course in this instance, it seems to me, is not to move an amendment to the motion that the Speaker do now leave the chair, but rather to present a bill to repeal the Emergency Powers Act, which could be done.
I do not want to add more to what I have just said. I just leave it to hon. members. The question in itself is one that is extremely difficult to deal with. I simply would not wish on this occasion to establish a precedent whereby, on a motion to go into supply, hon. members would propose an attack against a piece of legislation, something which they could do better by moving its repeal; that is, if we are to be guided by what is stated in our standing order 41, which reads in part as follows:
No member may reflect upon any vote of the house, except for the purpose of moving that such vote be rescinded.
We have always taken this rule to mean a vote in the same session. As I have said, there are doubts as to whether it is limited to votes in the same session. Then it has been seen that one cannot argue against or in any manner call into question a statute which is law because in doing so it imputes discredit to parliament. I submit these points to hon. members. Speaking for myself, I would prefer it if this amendment were to read:
This house desires to record its opinion that the administration of the powers granted to the governor in council under the Emergency Powers Act is repugnant to responsible parliamentary government.
There I would say it is a grievance that is complained of; you are complaining about the administration of the act. But to say that the powers granted to the governor in council are repugnant to responsible parliamentary government is, I think, to attack the principle of the Emergency Powers Act. It is a matter of attacking a statute or an existing law. If hon. members want to attack that act properly, I think they should do so by means of a motion to repeal the Emergency Powers Act.
I do not at this point wish to initiate a long debate on procedure. As I have indicated, the point is a difficult and complicated one. I do not wish to rule on the matter. I am simply asking those who have moved the

amendment to consider perhaps a rephrasing of their amendment. If they feel that they do not want to be as scrupulous as I would like to be at the moment, I am just going to let the matter rest and not deal with it any further.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) earlier in the day dealt with standing order 17, subparagraph 2 of which reads as follows:
Whenever government business has precedence, government orders may be called in such sequence as the government may think fit.
I think this standing order applies to the business that is on the order paper rather than to business that has not yet been placed on it. I think that is rather the meaning of that standing order.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did not submit rule 17 as being directly applicable. I submitted it only as an indication of a general theory that government business should be dealt with in the order in which the government saw fit to put it before the house. You will have noticed that I concluded by saying that if Your Honour felt that the rules were in too general terms to make it necessary for you to declare this motion out of order, I would ask our followers to vote it down.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The other point about which I am concerned is this. Once debate on this amendment which relates to the Emergency Powers Act has been concluded, if later a continuation in force of the Emergency Powers Act is proposed, hon. members will then be up against a standing order which says that one should not indulge in repetition. Of course, we cannot anticipate points of order. We shall have to deal with that matter when we reach it. However, hon. members can see what my difficulty will be at that moment.
If we carry on this debate, which offers such a wide scope, and review the Emergency Powers Act in all its ramifications, then suppose, before the session ends-and I should like students of procedure to examine that point, not discuss it now; I just submit it-that legislation is submitted to the house, what will I do if someone rises on a point of order and says that the argument the hon. member is presenting is one which we heard on the motion to go into supply, on such-and-such a date, and he is therefore repeating his argument.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if you would permit a question at that point? I wonder if that would not make it necessary for Your Honour to look at the records of last session when we had two debates on emergency powers, the first one on the bill to extend the Emergency Powers Act and 83276-204i

The fact that we had two
debates last year does not necessarily mean that we must indulge in the practice of having two debates on the same question this session.

Mr. Speaker, I think we can probably settle this matter quite shortly tonight in keeping with the course that you have indicated we should follow and that is not to enter into a long debate on procedure. Instead of rephrasing the amendment in exactly the terms which you have suggested, I wonder whether Your Honour would consider it would be satisfactory and would accomplish the purpose you had in mind if we rephrased it so that it would read:

It is a small modification of Your Honour's suggested wording.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Since the hon. member is in such a co-operative mood,-
He has no power of attorney.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

-may I suggest to him that
instead of the word "repugnant" he use the words "incompatible with"?
Quite.
