Mr. Speaker, I wish to raise a point of order as to the changing of an amendment once the amendment has become the property of the house. If you had not read the amendment to the house, Mr. Speaker, but had drawn to the attention of the movers of the amendment that you thought that, in its present wording, it was out of order, in my opinion that would have been your prerogative and your right and then they could amend it if they so wished. But once the amendment is read by you, Mr. Speaker, it becomes the property of the house and it cannot be amended without the consent of the house. I wish to draw to your attention that point which I think is a valid one.

Emergency Powers Act
Ivlr. Speaker: The hon. member is quite right.
Perhaps we could request the consent of the house.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Once I have made my observations on the question of rules and have asked those who are responsible for the amendment to consider changing certain words and once they have agreed, I must of course ask the house if they will agree to the change. If the hon. member objects, it cannot be done. He is quite right in that regard. But when we are trying to avoid declaring amendments out of order and instead to compose the various difficulties which may surround a point, I do not see why hon. members would not agree to the minor changes which are being suggested.

Mr. Speaker, before giving my consent to the change I should like to know what was the meaning of the word "repugnant" used by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew). That word has two meanings, a bad one and a philosophical one.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I have made my comments and I have suggested certain changes in the amendment to make it more in accordance with the spirit of our rules. The opposition has agreed to change it so that it reads:
this house desires to record its opinion that the exercise of the powers granted to the governor in council under the Emergency Powers Act is incompatible with responsible parliamentary government.
That is the suggestion. Do hon. members agree to this amendment being changed in the manner I have indicated?
Agreed.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot agree.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member does not agree then the amendment will remain as it is.

Mr. Speaker, if the things to which we took exception were always brought forward by unpleasant men it would be so much easier always to do the right thing and turn thumbs down on them. If the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) was only an unpleasant bully, instead of a pleasant gentleman, it would be very much easier to argue against this measure. But I wish to stress the fact that we should not be led away merely because we think at the present time that the administration of this measure is in the hands of people who will treat it, as far as they can, with discretion.
I shall have occasion later on to quote from a speech by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) and I hope what I shall quote will be treated more sympathetically than the quotation made by the hon. member

for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). The quotation will be relevant and it will stress the fact that we should look at the relevant principle and not merely consider personalities.
I was very surprised at some of the words used by the Prime Minister this afternoon because it seemed to me that he was relegating the opposition to a position where we hardly counted in this house at all. One of the remarks the Prime Minister used in criticizing the resolution was that it was an attempt "to anticipate something which may or may not happen". I believe that is true. But I would suggest, with deference to the Prime Minister, that that is true of an extraordinarily large number of things we have to do in this life. In a very large number of cases we have to exercise discretion on something which may or may not happen.
Another remark by the Prime Minister which struck me very forcibly was this: "It may be that between now and the time when it would be necessary to introduce legislation there may be happenings which will make it clear to everybody that the power granted under this Emergency Powers Act would not be required." That, I believe, is very true and I think it is perhaps the greatest justification of all for the opposition to seek to intervene now, through a valid expression of grievance, to bring public opinion to the point where it will not wish to have this act on the statute books any longer. In other words, I hope that what we are doing today may be one of the happenings which will make it clear to everybody that the powers granted under this act will not be required.
The Prime Minister has suggested that the fact that the act was not used should be an endorsement of the sincerity of the government in this matter. I believe in a certain sense that that is true, but on the other hand it is an equally good argument that the act is not required at all. That is the argument I wish to put forward.
The third remark by the Prime Minister, to which I wish to refer, is this: "It appertains to the government to decide in what year and at what time it"-that is government business -"will be dealt with." That, I believe, is an unassailable proposition, but if the inference from that is that until that time the opposition must just wait and see, that we should not take the initiative, then I doubt if this proposition would be supported by the Prime Minister to the end. There was a famous British statesman who got into considerable difficulty because he practised the slogan of "wait and see". At least, he was accused of doing so. I can see no reason whatever why

we should do so, nor can I see any reason why we should not press this resolution which reads:
this house desires to record its opinion that the powers granted to the governor in council under the Emergency Powers Act are repugnant to responsible parliamentary government.
That being our view, I suggest that it is not only our right but our duty to try to make that view prevail. Surely one of the chief duties ox an opposition is to try to make the public stop, look and listen. We do not succeed in that as often as we would like, but we have occasional successes which help us on our way. We certainly cannot achieve any success unless we are able to try to attract public opinion to our standard.
I would like in that connection to quote from an authority for whom, in one respect, I have the highest admiration, because he is a professor at Queen's University. The only qualification I have in my respect for him is that he is a little unsound politically; I mean that he follows the Liberal standard. But I would like to read what he has to say and I hope it will commend itself to the gentlemen across the floor. I hope they will agree with me that the remarks I am about to quote fully endorse my view as to the duties of an opposition. I am quoting from page 108 of Professor J. A. Corry's "Democratic Government and Politics". He says:
-there are always two or more sides to a story and the majority party has not heard all of the other side until the opposition has had Its say. Concession to the arguments of the opposition follows oftener than is generally believed.
I would like to believe that. I think perhaps he is a little bit enthusiastic there, but at any rate I think we should always assume not only that what we say will be listened to with courtesy, but that it will be weighed; and even though we do not succeed as often as we would like, nevertheless what we do say does have an effect. The quotation continues:
The public, despite its disillusionment, gets from the dramatic clash of parliamentary debate a grasp of the great issues of public policy which it cannot get in any other way until much larger resources are thrown into political education.
I believe the following is very important:
Finally, the new laws made each year are only a tiny fraction of the old ones which are being administered day by day. Oppressive, wasteful, or neglectful administration will be a black mark against the party which presently controls the executive power if its behaviour can be given wide publicity.
I suggest that what Professor Corry outlines there covers fully the task we are seeking to discharge today, namely, to come to the House of Commons in the hope that public opinion is moving, in the hope that before long it will have moved to the point
Emergency Powers Act where, as the Prime Minister said, it may not be necessary-which in other words means the government will come to the conclusion it will not be necessary-to continue this legislation. I hope the fact that we have debated this today may have a very definite impact upon the government's attitude in this matter. If it has, then I think we shall have discharged our duty as an opposition successfully; and if it has not we shall have discharged our duty as an opposition not so successfully.
I want to read very briefly from the act itself just to remind people of the breadth of the authority. I think we all have to recognize that we have got used to the exercise of wide powers. There is a great danger that we in the opposition get far too used to it. I am quite certain that such powers must be very tempting indeed to any government because I am quite sure that busy ministers must find discussions in the House of Commons often very tiresome. They must often regard them as perilously near a waste of time. They would hardly be human if they did not feel they had an unusual allotment of wisdom, and so I think it is almost too much to expect that they will be always on the alert to cut down their own powers. I would think it would be unfair. I hope 1 never find myself, as a member of the opposition, suggesting that it is fair to expect members of the government to cut down their own powers. Therefore we are the only people who can bring the importance of their being cut down to their attention, always in the hope that we may have an effect, sometimes when we least expect it. But I do want to read one recital from the act which is as follows:
And whereas it is essential that emergency powers be conferred to enable measures to be taken as urgently required from time to time to carry out adequate defence preparations, to regulate the economy of Canada to meet the needs of defence . . .
Having just read those words, I find it extremely difficult, Mr. Speaker, to understand why some of the orders in council passed since 1951 needed to be passed. They do not seem to me to be terribly emergent. I will make reference to one or two of them, and I would have thought they were passed not because there was a great emergency, other than to save the time and effort of the ministers, but because it was a very nice convenient way of dealing with the matter through this act rather than through what I suggest was the relevant act, which would have had to be brought back into the House of Commons and debated, with a resolution and three readings and all the rights of the minority, which are so precious to the

Emergency Powers Act minority and so important to our constitution but which I am equally sure sometimes become a little tiresome to government.
I find that an order in council was passed on December 6, 1951 exempting from customs duties personal gifts of a value not exceeding $25 from members of the Canadian forces serving abroad and addressed to relatives or friends in Canada. It does seem to me that the proper place to have done that was not under the Emergency Powers Act but under the relevant act, which I suppose is the Customs Act. I find one or two other cases. Here is one dealing with the licensing of pilots under the Aeronautics Act. I would have thought the Aeronautics Act might have been wide enough to deal with that. I find an order in council extending the provisions of the Defence Services Pension Act, and so on.
I suggest that those are instances of what happens when you get powers nicely concentrated with such broad words that, as the lawyers say, you can do almost anything except make a man a woman or a woman a man. I suggest that such powers are not desirable except in times of great emergency. Nobody denies that we are living in a world which is not free from some emergency and if there were no other way, if there were no other power available I might find it much more difficult to argue against this measure and to say what I am saying. But of course we are all aware of the War Measures Act. We are all aware that power can be invoked but that it is suggested that to do so would perhaps create a condition of alarm which would be undesirable. That, at any rate, is the argument that has been put forward.
I referred to the fact that a year ago we sought to have this act not renewed. At that time we were given various reasons, some worse than others. When the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) asked us to be content because any orders in council passed would subsequently be tabled and we would then have every chance to have them abrogated if we wished, I thought he was attributing to us powers which we really do not seem to have because, as I said before the dinner recess, I cannot remember cases where, after the government has taken action in that way, they have been prepared to recede. I should think it extremely unlikely that I or anyone else in the house will live to see that.
Of course the great objection to orders in council, as has been said so many times, is that there is no publicity. No one knows in advance what is going on. After the event we are faced with publicity, yes, so that we know what has been going on, but I think


no one who looks at things in a matter of fact way will expect that it will be possible for us even to have such matters seriously debated. I think that would be far too much to expect.
We are asked to regard this power as something about which no one really needs to get very worried. The Prime Minister has told us that during his journey he found that a good many countries regarded our political enlightenment and our state of freedom with admiration. I can quite believe that. Of course one would need to know more about the state of the countries themselves. It may be it was not a very great compliment. But on the other hand no one is going to deny that we in this country do not live in a state of oppression or anything of that kind. But we come back to the fact that when legislation is left on the statute books which contains such great powers these powers may be quite innocuous in ordinary times and may be left there because nobody thinks it worth while to try to dispose of them, but we all know that in countries where freedom has been lost it was lost because people grew careless and because they did not take the trouble in more quiet times to see that such legislation was kept down to the minimum.
I want to refer briefly to a writer who has written something about the state of affairs in the United Kingdom. I always feel that the United Kingdom, with its centuries of common tradition, with its homogeneous population, with its traditions of freedom, with all the safeguards it has against loss of freedom, has an enviable position, and when I find that serious people in the United Kingdom are warning against the very same thing we are trying to warn against then I think it is well worth while to stop, look and listen. I propose to put a very short quotation on the record from a book I have in my hand entitled "The Passing of Parliament", the author being Professor Keeton, professor of English law at University College, London. I want to read briefly from page 199 of his book. In a way these are strange words coming from a serious Englishman, and I read them with surprise. I think we should take them seriously and I think they point a wise course for ourselves. He says:
The problem which therefore faces all peoples which are still attached to the democratic way of life is to find some means of curbing the power of the executive, and preventing it from usurping the entire functions of government. The nineteenth century assumption that this would be achieved by successive extensions of the franchise has proved completely fallacious.
I do not think a single man in this house would challenge that statement, the idea that by a mere extension of the franchise we were going to increase and make more strict the

public control over the executive. I do not believe anyone adheres to that idea today. I continue to quote from Keeton:
The executive, as it has ventured to interfere increasingly with the lives of its subjects, has at the same time taken care to ensure that its servants and dependents (including the state-monopolies) are removed from the sphere of popular control. Its techniques grow ever more audacious. Today, in Britain, it is not only that wide powers of legislation, in fact if not in theory immune from parliamentary control, have been granted to the departments. In addition, these powers in turn are habitually delegated by the departments to its own agents.
As I had occasion the other afternoon to point out when we had the export-import bill before us, the definition of "minister" included, as I recall it, anyone to whom he delegated the power.
Instances of sub-delegation to the fourth and fifth degree are not uncommon. In addition, the case of Earl Fitzwilliam's Wentworth Estates Co. v. Minister of Town and Country Planning illustrates how what has been called departmental quasi-legislation by circulars and explanatory memoranda, can acquire compulsive force.
I just want to add one more citation from page 201.
It is plain, therefore, that we are already approaching the dangerous half-light in which the boundaries of what is legal and what is not are barely perceptible.
I just want to go back for a moment, Mr. Speaker, to say that although we are assured there will be no trespassing on the powers given, I suggest that those orders in council to which I made specific reference were never intended to come under this act. They should have been dealt with under the relevant acts concerned. This just shows us how broad powers, which are such an easy method by which to do business, will be used more and more freely as time goes on.
As I tried to show a while ago, Mr. Speaker, I think one of the main duties of the opposition is to get the public to stop, look, and listen, and we try to make the public in this case believe that when we say this legislation is incompatible with responsible parliamentary government, we are saying what is true. We must hope that the public will come to our aid when we say there is no need for this kind of legislation. You can reach the necessary results in other ways. There is no need for leaving on the statute books legislation that it is quite clear is not necessary. I know the argument which has been used that standby legislation is good; that it is often useful to have a club behind your back. I do not think that is a sound argument for legislation. I hope that argument will not be made in this debate, although it has been made in this house. I can quite see that at times it might be convenient, but I believe it to
Emergency Powers Act be one of the most unsound reasons for legislation and one which we should regard with the greatest possible suspicion.
There is one other thing I want to mention, and this is where I can read from an article written by the hon. member for Vancouver South which appeared in the Vancouver Sun on February 19, 1953. I quoted from this article when I spoke on this subject a year ago, and welcomed the statement which had been made by the present member for Vancouver South. I quoted him with considerable satisfaction. I hope he is not going to let me down in what I am going to quote now. He says this, as it appeared at page 3309 of Hansard for March 26, 1953:
It is no doubt true that there will be no serious abuse of the emergency powers, if they are granted for another year. But it is worth remembering that neither this Prime Minister nor this government will last forever.
That is quite an admission from a member sitting on the opposite benches. I suppose he would never have said that if he had been a Liberal member at the time. Then he goes on:
Nobody knows who will head our government a year hence. A bad principle is a bad principle- and this is a very bad principle. A bad precedent is a bad precedent-and this is a very bad precedent.
Those words seemed to me to be wise a year ago, and I imagine that a year ago they seemed to be wise to him. I hope he will say nothing to undermine them in any way.
Now, Mr. Speaker, for myself I am glad this subject has been brought up. I only wish we had loud speakers loud enough so we could din this into the ear of every voter. I recall that a year ago this measure produced a phenomenon which has almost never happened in this house, and that is that two members sitting on the government benches voted against the government. It reminds me of a very interesting comment on our house that was made the other day by an observer temporarily here from England. He said one thing that interested me greatly. He had this comment to make about the government party. As I am going to tell in some detail what he said about the government, I perhaps had better be frank enough to say that what he said about the opposition was not entirely to my liking, either.
About the government, he said something that goes to the very root of parliamentary government. He said that if in the British house you had a majority such as you have in your house there would be all kinds of little ginger groups, all kinds of people with views of their own that they wanted to express. You could not possibly discipline them as well as they are disciplined in your house.

Emergency Powers Act
I mention that just to conclude with the hope that, as a year ago when this measure was before us there were members on the government side who voted with us, possibly that phenomenon may happen again because it seems to me it would be a healthy and wholesome thing to happen in this house.

This matter, Mr. Speaker, is very easy to understand. The Emergency Powers Act will cease to exist on May 31 next unless it is renewed in the meantime. Those are the facts. What surprised me very much was that the first motion sponsored by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) after the renewal of confidence that has been given to him by his supporters was this very motion which is untimely, in fact it is premature, uncalled for and futile.
What surprised me more than that was that it was supported by my very good friend, the hon. member for Vancouver -Quadra (Mr. Green), who was one of two Conservative members of parliament at the time who accompanied their former leader, Lord Bennett, to the union station. He had tears in his eyes. My hon. friend will remember that he was accompanied at the station by the late Dave Spence. They were the only two there; and poor Mr. Bennett had tears in his eyes, thinking that Dufferin-Simcoe was not there, Dufferin-Simcoe whom he had created a privy councillor.

speechtext: Order. I do not think that the fact that someone was accompanied by hon. members at the union station has much relevancy to the amendment now before the house. And, further, the hon. member should refer to another member by calling him "the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe" and not simply "Dufferin-Simcoe".

On a question of privilege; I am sure my good friend, the hon. member for Temiscouata, would not wish to be in error. Actually there were three of us who saw Mr. Bennett off. It was very, very, early in the morning, and the rest of the party had said good-bye to him the night before.
I thank my hon. friend for his correction, but I suggest that he look at the newspaper files and he will see that he was alone, with Dave Spence.
The newspapers are not always right.

I am through with the sad part of past recollections. Now, sir, at the present time we have legislation which may be repealed or which may be continued. To


act with wisdom it is necessary for the government to take matters under advisement, just the same as judges do before rendering their judgments.
The Leader of the Opposition is far from being a mind reader. He does not know at all what happens behind the closed doors of the privy council-unless he peeks through the keyhole; I do not insinuate that he does that-although some do, some from his own party. I am not going to dot the "i's" and cross the "t's", but I refer to actual facts which are well known to all members in the house.
Now, what was in the speech of the Leader of the Opposition? What was in the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) who supported the amendment? The only ground upon which the Leader of the Opposition based his argument was the fact that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) had come with an order in council when the question of extending the Emergency Powers Act legislation was before the house.
Then, besides that, he spoke about the rule of law. What does he know about it? He spoke about the fundamentals of parliamentary practice. What does he know about them? He spoke about things which are foreign to him, and I shall prove it very clearly. The Leader of the Opposition quoted some extracts from speeches delivered in the house in 1921 by Mr. Mackenzie King when the Meighen government was in office, and in 1935 when the Bennett government was in office.
Mr. King was heaping anathema on the Meighen government and the Bennett government, which were supported by the Leader of the Opposition. Did he say then that Mr. Mackenzie King was a great man? No. He criticized Mackenzie King at the time-and I was supporting Mackenzie King. He now quotes and praises the anathema of Mackenzie King against the Meighen government and the Bennett government.
With the experience I have in parliament, an experience much longer than that of the Leader of the Opposition, may I give him a piece of advice. When I was fighting Bennett, he was an appointee of Howard Ferguson, holding the office in Ontario of commissioner of securities. I will give him this piece of advice: "Let the dead bury their dead".
You should have given them advice in Elgin and Peel.

I will tell my hon. friend that the Leader of the Opposition, who has been

boasting that he would make progress, has made no progress at the by-elections today. It would be better for the hon. member not to interrupt too much, because-let me tell him that I can use a secret weapon more deadly or deadlier than the one Samson used when fighting the Tories of his time, the Philistines.

speechtext: Order. It may be that the house would prefer to listen to the remarks of the hon. member, although they are somewhat foreign to the amendment before us. However it is my duty to call the attention of the hon. member to the fact that he must come back to the question under debate.
I said it, sir, I used the word "Tory".
Get off the comic page.

Now, sir, here is a gentleman -and I say that because, personally, as a private individual, he is a gentleman, and this gentleman-honourable gentleman-has used the denunciation of his party by the leader of the Liberal party as an argument in protest against legislation which is actually in force. He says: This debate is not academic. Well, where does his amendment lead? It leads to nowhere; it is a trip to nowhere. And if the hon. gentleman knew the rule of law, if he knew parliamentary practice, if he knew British parliamentary practice, he would have done as Your Honour suggested. Instead of sponsoring a silly amendment like this he would have sponsored a bill, and would have been on record to show his sincerity by asking for the repeal of the legislation he complains about.
Far from it. He went to great length to say that hon. members were grimacing; that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) was grimacing. And he was very much high-hat with no less a gentleman than the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Habel). He may hear from him in due course. I am not the only one who can speak to him through the chair. Well, that was it.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra made another excellent argument. He said that the speech of the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) was foolish. He said it two or three times. What arguments! What powerful arguments to crush the Liberal party! Imagine! And they are surprised that the people do not take them seriously. They have no political acumen, not the least bit of it. It is unfortunate. I will chide the opposition to be strong; I will chide the opposition to be worthy of its functions, to establish the rule of law and to maintain the best traditions of parliamentary practice.
Emergency Powers Act What can we expect? We had the performance this afternoon; grimacing, foolish, that is all.
There is more to it. It is the very designation of the act, the Emergency Powers Act. It is a very important one. Is the hon. gentleman who sponsored the amendment ready to say that there is no emergency in the world at the present time? Is the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra ready to say that there is no emergency on the coast of British Columbia when he has told us so many times that he is concerned about the invasion of the Pacific? Nobody spoke about it as much as he did, and it was a long time before the Korean war. Do they know what is an emergency? Do they realize that at the present time the condition of the world is giving concern to people who have more experience than both of them put together? And here just for political purposes they make an attack on the government. They come with an olive branch saying that they are like the doves that came out of Noah's ark. They come with an olive branch of peace. They are not serious. The Canadian people do not consider them serious. They realized at the last election that the leadership of the Conservative party was not-

Mr. Speaker, the Leader of Opposition (Mr. Drew) said at a meeting of eight people in Verdun-Montreal that the supporters of the government were sheep. I want to show him that there are rams among the supporters.
Also bores.

We are spoken of as members who follow blindly the dictates of the government. We have confidence in the government and we have no confidence in the official opposition. Wait and see. That was the victorious answer of Herbert Asquith to the Tories of his time and I am very glad that my hon. friend is not one. I say that in all sincerity. I am for the maintenance of the privileges of parliament, and not only of parliament as an abstract body but of each member of the House of Commons. To recall old memories, I remember when old Mr. Bruce of Toronto could not speak at one time, and I took his defence-although I did not agree with him-because I wanted him to have the right to say what he thought right, probably. We are all for the defence of our institutions, of the privileges of parliament, and it is precisely on account of that that it is my duty to oppose very strongly the futile amendment of the Leader of the Opposition.
I have said enough for the time being. My concluding words will be that as a Liberal I am glad to see him as Leader of the Opposition once more, because when the Tories select a leader they always choose the wrong one.

I always
appreciate listening to the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) who does enliven the house with his delightful humour. When he made reference today to the jaw bone used on a previous occasion I might say that his own would give great competition in that respect.
This debate, Mr. Speaker, in my opinion, has become very academic because what we have in essence is an amendment protesting a statute which apparently is not in practical operation. I was rather surprised to hear the hon. member who has just taken his seat say that the government requires this legislation in the case of an emergency such as an invasion of this country. Now of course that is stretching it to the breaking point because we all know that the War Measures Act is still in operation, or could be called into operation at any time, and that would be the statute under which the government could meet any emergency. The Emergency Powers Act, about which this amendment protests, apparently has not been used since it was last endorsed by this parliament. If I


understood the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) correctly, I understood him to say it has not been used since the last time it came before the house.
That being so, it seems rather strange that there should be such a great deal of breastbeating about the whole thing. In addition to that, I think it has now been made clear that the debate is getting to the point where the members on the government side and the members of the official opposition are ready to admit that it all depends on which side of the house you happen to be sitting which attitude you are going to take. First we have the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) saying, in his delightful manner, that he is not surprised that the opposition is criticizing the government for arrogating unto itself great powers because if he were in the opposition he would be inclined to do the same thing. Then a little later the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Maedonnell) made the statement that he is not surprised that the government does not wish to reduce its own powers, because if he were in their position he would not want to do that either. So there we have it. It depends on whether hon. members happen to be on the government side or in the official opposition as to the attitude they take.
On the point that would really matter, namely whether either the members who support the government or the members of the official opposition are prepared to use any of these emergency powers to bring about any changes which would be to the benefit of the country as a whole in order to meet any of the existing emergencies, I think it is now becoming clear that they do not disagree; they are both for the status quo, and it appears to me that they are almost in violent agreement on that point. For example, wide powers are given to the government under the act. I admit that. Let me also say-and I am speaking for myself -that I have no objection to wide powers being given to the government by this parliament or by any parliament provided those powers are used for the purpose of meeting real emergencies and bringing about solutions to them in the interests of the general public welfare.
Referring to the act itself, we find in section 2, paragraphs (d) and (e) and further down in subsection 3, powers that would enable the government to meet almost any ordinary emergency, with perhaps the exception of war. For example, in paragraph (d) such things are covered as transportation by land, air or water and the control of the transport of persons and

things. Then in paragraph (e) such things are covered as trading, exportation, importation, production and manufacture. Then in subsection 3 we find this provision:
All orders and regulations made under or pursuant to authority conferred under this act have the force of law while this act is in force.
That indicates that the powers granted there are fairly wide. But the question is this: What has the government done or what does it propose to do to make use of these powers in order to meet some of the emergencies which are before the country today?
I have not heard at this point whether the government intends to use any of these powers. We have been told that in the past year they have not been used; on such issues that face this country as inflation, for example, we have been told that the government has not the ordinary powers to reimpose price control. There are such issues as unemployment. Then again we are told that owing to our constitutional position the government lacks the power effectively to do anything about it. We are faced with a great grain surplus in western Canada. Again, no action. There is a question of social security.
Only today we have an example of the blinding speed with which the government moves, when the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) tells us that, even though as far back as twelve months ago we had a forecast of certain legislation dealing with pensions for crippled persons, to date he is not able to say when it is going to come before the house; and it may not come into operation until the end of 1954. That situation indicates that the government is not using even the ordinary powers and procedures which they have at their command and that the Emergency Powers Act in itself is only an adornment. As far as I can see, the only purpose it has been serving in the past year has been to gratify the ego of the government because it certainly has not been used to meet any of the emergencies which have arisen and which are facing the country. That is why I say I believe this debate is academic in the extreme. With all due respect, I say that the official opposition are protesting against something which the government claims they are not doing.
Going back over some of the debates in the past we find, of course, that when the Liberal party was in opposition the speeches made by Liberal members on that occasion about some of the orders in council and some of the legislation passed by the then administration were almost word for word what we 83276-205i
Emergency Powers Act hear from the official opposition today. I submit that the real questions before us are being sidetracked and forgotten in the midst of this flurry of excitement about an inoperative piece of legislation. As I looked back, it just struck me that in 1951, when this act was being put through this parliament, or in the same year, there appeared in the Western Producer, which is a widely-read weekly paper in western Canada, an editorial which should almost be required reading for every member of the government. It is dated October 11, 1951. I should like to quote just one short paragraph in order to point out what should have been engaging the thinking of this parliament and of the government instead of pretending that something is going to be done under powers which they now tell us have not been used. Here is the opinion expressed by that paper:
It is only too distressingly evident that the talk of a better, a more just economic order has not gone beyond the talking stage. The present prosperity and the various large-scale government undertakings for aiding those in need are in reality a false front. They owe their existence to the huge and growing activities devoted to defence and preparation for war. We are living in a war economy. To realize this let the reader try to envisage what would happen if by some miracle sure and certain peaceful understanding between the nations of the world were suddenly established. That glorious news would be followed by so calamitous a depression that it is hard to believe that our economy would survive it. For it would mean a sudden halt to all armament production, thousands of factories would be closed, hundreds of thousands thrown out of work. We strive and pray for real and lasting peace yet ignore or are completely unprepared to meet the catastrophic shock to our whole economy which would be the inevitable result of real enduring peace.
That is a challenging editorial and I think it underlines what I have been leading up to or have been attempting to say, namely that unless the government is prepared to meet the emergencies of the day, to do some long-range planning to meet the situations which may arise, legislation of this sort serves no purpose. Those situations are already casting their shadows before them. The unemployment figures themselves indicate that what the editorial said in 1951 was only too true. We have cut back national defence spending by only a small amount, both in Canada and the United States, but its effect is already being widely felt. What has the government to put in its place?
Those are the real issues facing this country, not only today but in the years to come. Those are the things that we in this parliament should be debating and planning for, not wasting our time and energy fighting about an Emergency Powers Act which was

Emergency Powers Act passed in 1951, which was renewed year after year and which the Prime Minister now tells us was not even used. Why worry about something which is not even being used? So far as I am concerned, I feel that the government has not made the best possible use of the resources they have had at their command. For my part I would say that it is of no use to carry on the statute books legislation of this nature which appears to be only for the purpose of pretending that something is going to be done when there is an emergency, that the emergency is recognized, and that the government is prepared to do something about it. That is not the case.
I appeal to the government on the grounds that the issues facing the country today are small in comparison with what they will be in two years' time. I hope I may be proved wrong, but that is what I believe at the present time. Instead of cluttering up the statute books with emergency powers and acts of parliament which are never used, I say let us make use of the legislation which already exists, let us make use of the facilities we already have, and let us do some planning for the future. Let us prevent a catastrophe in which even wider powers may be sought by this government.

Mr. Speaker, I believe there is a principle involved in this motion now before the house which requires serious consideration. I did not follow the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) who has just spoken in many of his arguments, and particularly in regard to that in which he claimed that if the positions were reversed in this house and the opposition sat on the treasury benches the same powers now reposing in the government would be sought by the opposition. I do not believe that suggestion has been made by any hon. member of the opposition so far. Nor did I follow the hon. member in his argument that because the Emergency Powers Act has not been frequently used we should pay no attention to it.
I believe it is the duty of parliament to examine anything in the nature of extended powers asked for by the government, and to examine whether these powers are necessary. The amendment now before the house is simply the medium by which a redress of grievance is being sought, and a medium by which the opposition may draw to the attention of the people of Canada the fact that the power vested in the executive is greater than it need be, and that that power should be checked.
There has been considerable criticism in recent years of the decline in the power of

parliament and the corresponding increase in the power of the cabinet. Many commentators on political affairs have written on that aspect of the matter, and it has been discussed, of course, in the House of Commons on many occasions.
Earlier this evening my colleague, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), quoted from a work by Professor Corry. I would also like to quote a passage from page 649 of the same volume. The professor was dealing with the problem of whether the democracies are travelling along the road towards dictatorship, and he was also dealing with this problem of the decline in the power of parliament and the growth in the power of the executive. The professor has this to say:
Yet the democracies are still a long way from such a concentration of power-
That is, compared with a dictatorship.
-and it is open to them to halt these trends before they reach the monolithic state. There is now much more concentration of power in the democratic governmental structure than there was in 1900 and this is not without its alarming aspects. But it is not necessarily beyond human ingenuity to find improved methods of control as counterpoises to the aggrandizement of the executive and the growing predominance of national over local, and state or provincial, governments.
That, the professor says, is the crux of the matter. This particular act to which we have been referring simply points up the attitude of the executive as an attempt to encroach still further upon the prerogatives of parliament. It is the function of the opposition to draw attention to that encroachment.
This afternoon the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) dealt with some of the functions of the opposition as he saw them, and I believe that in many of his remarks he was perfectly accurate. He suggested it was the function of the opposition to harass the government, attack the ministers, and to criticize and oppose. In that statement he is on very firm ground.
Sir Ivor Jennings, who has written a very useful book entitled, "Cabinet Government" based on parliamentary experience in the United Kingdom, has something to say with regard to the function of the opposition. I believe what he says is of importance because there is often a misunderstanding in the public mind and sometimes in this house as to the function of the opposition. But this is what he has to say on page 439 of his book: It is not untrue to say that the most important part of parliament is the opposition in the House of Commons. The function of parliament is not to govern but to criticize. Its criticism, too, is directed not so much towards a fundamental modification of the government's policy as towards the education of public opinion. The government's majority exists to support the government. The function of

the opposition is to secure a majority against the government at the next general election and thus to replace the government. This does not imply that a government may not be defeated in the House of Commons. Nor does it imply that parliamentary criticism may not persuade the government to modify, or even to withdraw, its proposals. These qualifications are important; but they do not destroy the truth of the principle that the government governs and the opposition criticizes. Failure to understand this simple principle is one of the causes of the failure of so many of the progeny of the mother of parliaments and of the supersession of parliamentary government by dictatorships.
Another remark by the Secretary of State attracted my attention. He said the function of the opposition was to criticize and oppose, and he rejected any idea of joint responsibility. Yet I suggest there are occasions when there is some joint responsibility in the House of Commons. For example, we find a certain measure of that joint responsibility in the realm of external affairs, and the view has been adopted here that in order to present a united front to the rest of the world on external affairs there should be no marked difference of opinion in this house. That would be a sound approach if full information was given to the opposition.
Sir Ivor Jennings deals with that point on page 465 of his book and I would like to quote. Speaking of the opposition he said:
Sometimes, indeed, it agrees not to oppose. This is particularly true of foreign affairs. For the enmity within is as nothing compared with the enmity without. The suggestion that the nation is divided gives encouragement to enemies abroad.
He then goes on to give examples from the British House of Commons where the opposition was taken into the confidence of the government so that a united front in foreign affairs might be presented. Sir Ivor Jennings points out that the giving of information to the opposition was particularly necessary where secret agreements prevailed so that should there be a change in government the incoming government would be aware of these obligations. I therefore suggest that there are occasions on which there is a certain measure of joint responsibility. Sir Ivor also points out on page 466:
Further, agreement may be made with the opposition to secure the settlement of a question which has so long divided political parties that an agreed solution becomes necessary.
We in this country may not have had anything as critical as that, but that has been the English experience. There is another reference, and this is related to the whole question of the powers which the executive has gradually been taking to itself within the House of Commons. The Secretary of State said that the government derives its power from the House of Commons and modified it to say, from a group within the House of Commons, which is of course
Emergency Powers Act accurate. The government derives its power actually from the party. Parliamentary government as it existed in the nineteenth century has been modified in the twentieth century to become, as Professor Corry calls it, party government. That fact must be recognized. The cabinet is supported by the party system and is dependent upon it to maintain itself in office. For example, Jennings says on page 439:
It is said that the House of Commons controls parliament.
Theoretically that is so because measures have to be passed by parliament, but in actual fact the control rests elsewhere. He goes on to say:
But, in truth, the fundamental criticism of the proposition is that it ignores the party system and thus ignores the fact that, through the party system, it is the government that controls the House of Commons.
The Secretary of State, in dealing with the question of the government not disclosing certain information on motions for the production of papers, went on to suggest that it was not the members on the treasury benches who voted down such motions but that it was the house that did so. But surely that is ignoring the party system completely. Members who are supporting the treasury benches naturally are not going to vote against their leaders in the House of Commons unless they wish to face disaster. Our system depends on party government and the party must remain intact or the gover-ment fails to maintain its position. That, I think, is a fact which is sometimes overlooked. The power of the executive depends of course upon the solidarity that it can maintain within its party in the House of Commons. For example, consider this passage on page 441 of Mr. Jennings' book:
The member of parliament is thus returned to support a party. He recognizes his party obligations by receipt of the "whip"; if he disagrees with the party policy on a particular matter, he may abstain from voting. Occasionally, perhaps, he votes against his party. If he does so too frequently, he loses the "whip"; and this means probably, the loss of party support at the next election. Without that support, he will probably not be elected. Also, his party loyalty as well as his self-interest will induce him normally to vote with the party. . . Above all, a supporter of the government is very unlikely to take any step which will defeat the government. For, if it is defeated on a major issue, it will resign or dissolve parliament. If it resigns, he has assisted the formation of a government by the opposition, which is, ex hypothesi, worse than that which he was elected to support. If parliament is dissolved, he will have to undergo the trouble and possibly the expense of an election; and it may not be certain that he will be re-elected.
Consequently, as the Secretary of State said, the members of the treasury benches certainly do not vote down these motions

Emergency Powers Act themselves. They vote them down with the support of the party behind them. It is thoroughly understood here that that is what happens, and we would be the most surprised people on earth if the treasury benches rose in support of a measure and all their supporters took the opposite stand. The party system is thoroughly established as part of our system of parliamentary government, and it is on that party system that the executive is dependent for its support.
With regard to the Emergency Powers Act, I have never been able to see the necessity for such additional powers being sought by the executive. I have never been able to see any force in the argument, "Oh well, you can trust us; we will not misuse our powers." I see no force in the argument, "we have not used them very often". We had an example last year of the use of the Emergency Powers Act in the tabling of an order in council under that legislation while parliament was still sitting. We have the example of a secret order in council which apparently stands or falls with the Emergency Powers Act. It is my opinion that there should never be in Canada such a thing as a secret order in council. I do not think that under our democracy secrecy is necessary along that line.
If it is important that something should be withheld from public knowledge, then that would be one of the instances when at least the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and the leaders of the other opposition parties should have some information as to a matter of such importance. The government has power without passing legislation such as the Emergency Powers Act. The experience of the British house is a case in point. Jennings is very useful in directing our attention to that. At page 447 he says:
British governments are in tact expected to govern. If necessary, they are expected to act even when they have no legal powers. They can rely on their majorities and on the common sense of the house to rectify their acts. There is and can be no limitation on retroactive legislation. A government can act first and ask for approval afterwards. It can declare war though it has not the power to place the forces on a war footing though it is the duty of the government to summon parliament at once.
May I interject there to say that in 1939 the services in Canada were placed on a war footing almost two weeks before parliament assembled and declared war against the enemy. Was there any question at that time about the government exercising power that was not inherent in its prerogative? I do not think so. That met with the good sense of the people of Canada and of members of the House of Commons. The government has these powers without passing legislation


such as the particular act that has been mentioned tonight. But Professor Jennings goes on to point out that when such actions are taken by the government, the immediate summoning of parliament is necessary so that it may be informed and may give its approval of the acts of the government.
The weakness in the Emergency Powers Act, as I see it, is that the government may act without summoning parliament and therefore can keep from the people of the country information that should be available in a democracy. Surely, as we pointed out earlier this afternoon, there is no longer any difficulty about summoning parliament rather quickly. Transportation has developed to such an extent that the house can be called together with dispatch. Why, therefore, grant to the cabinet the power to act without parliament being called to pass on those decisions? It could so happen that five months might elapse after action taken by the cabinet under the Emergency Powers Act, and parliament would not receive the information until it had again been convened.
Under the practice as we have known it in the past, established over the centuries in the great tradition of British parliamentary democracy, governments are certainly expected to act and make decisions, then to have their acts ratified as quickly as possible by parliament. The information is conveyed to parliament, and through parliament to the people. It is against this seeking of power by the cabinet that we make this protest. We make this protest fulfilling the function of the opposition, and hopeful that we may influence the government to restrict its desire for power.
We are still more hopeful that we may catch the ear of the people and inform them of what is being done here; inform them that their liberties are in danger. It is essential that our parliamentary system be maintained, that our democratic institutions be maintained in their full vigour. It is the duty of the opposition to draw attention at any time that it observes the power of the House of Commons is being diminished in any way by an increase in the power of the executive.

On
the amendment that is now before the house, Mr. Speaker, I find myself in the position of being on the horns of a dilemma. I am unalterably opposed to emergency powers being in the hands of the governor general in council. I cannot see the reason for any such need. It is my honour to come from a constituency in Vancouver. From Vancouver, on the far western coast, we can come to Ottawa by aeroplane in about thirteen

hours; by train, we can be here in four days and three nights. I cannot conceive of such an emergency as would require emergency powers in peacetime, or why any decision of the government could not be submitted to parliament itself.
I have an objection to special powers. I can remember back in 1934 when a Liberal premier in British Columbia introduced the special powers act, known as the S.P.A. Later it became known as the supreme provincial asininity. In that act every power of parliament was taken into the hands of a lieutenant governor in council in British Columbia. I want to admit that the powers were never once used in any way whatever, and several years later the act was repealed. But I cannot see any reason for these strict emergency powers being in the hands of the governor general in council.
Whilst I condemn very much in principle the transference of the powers of parliament on an emergency basis into the hands of the governor general in council, at the same time I condemn the method whereby the official opposition has drawn this matter to the attention of the house. It is my personal opinion that it has been done completely on the basis of political expediency. In my estimation it could have been done on the basis of principle by using other methods. This afternoon I was interested in listening closely to the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew). I agree completely with the principles that he espouses, but I do not agree with all the arguments that he used. If my memory serves me correctly, when he spoke about dictatorship and bureaucracy he should have recalled that the greatest instance we ever had of dictatorship and bureaucracy was under a Conservative government under the late R. B. Bennett. During the election campaign he told us he was going to blast his way into the markets of the world, and his word was accepted by the electors of Canada. The depression continued, and the only blasting was that he blasted himself into an earldom in Great Britain.
These remarks may seem rather strange coming from a member sitting in the opposition. I am not speaking from the brief experience I have had here, but from twenty years' experience as a public servant. I will admit that for perhaps the first three or four years that I had the honour of being a public servant I went after the government from the opposition side. However, I learned a lesson and a principle. The principle was, and I still maintain it, that I will never say anything from the opposition side in parliament, denouncing the government or demanding action from the government, that I do not
Emergency Powers Act think I could put into effect if I were on the opposite side of the house. I do not believe the official opposition is attacking this matter from that basis.
I was most interested in the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) this afternoon. I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that on this matter of the amendment now before us I believe the Prime Minister made a statesmanlike reply. He stated that there is now on the statute books the Emergency Powers Act, and it will remain there until the end of May. The government has not yet made up its mind what it is going to do. I do not like to try to be a prophet, but I do not believe the government is going to ask for the continuation of that measure. As I said, that act will be in effect until the end of May. If the government in its wisdom does not introduce a bill that measure automatically dies.
So all the hours, and the thousands of dollars we have cost the taxpayers this afternoon, go out the window. If the government, in its stupidity, brings in a continuation, we will then have the opportunity, when it brings in the bill, to have a debate; when we know what they have in mind. We can debate it then, as we have been discussing the matter this afternoon.
So perhaps, Mr. Speaker, you will understand what I mean when I say that I am on the horns of a dilemma. In principle I am unalterably opposed to this transference of the powers of parliament to the executive, the cabinet. I am unalterably opposed to that. At the same time I am also unalterably opposed to the method in which this question is now raised in the House of Commons, and the hours of time it has taken up.
So, sir, I shall make my position clear: If the government does not bring in a bill for the continuation of this measure, then I say, "more power and more credit to them". I do not think it is necessary. If an emergency arises, parliament can be called inside of a week. Then if the government does bring in a bill, I intend to have something to say, and it will be at far greater length than I have spoken now.
However, an amendment is now before the house. It has not been ruled out of order. If I may say so, sir, that is the only criticism I have of the Prime Minister. I think he made an interesting, statesmanlike, practical and logical presentation this afternoon, but he did not carry it to its ultimate conclusion of asking you, sir, to decide whether or not the amendment is in order. I think he should have. However, that was his business, not mine.

I do think, sir, that we should get to a vote. Let us wait until the matter comes up, and we will speak on the government's action at that time.

Before the hon. member speaks, perhaps I should comment briefly on the last sentence of the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch). It is the duty of the Speaker to make up his mind as to whether a motion is or is not in order. That is his duty, no matter who, from either side of the house, asks for a ruling. I do not think the hon. member's statement should remain without some comment on my part.
If I have not decided that the amendment is out of order, it is because I have not found sufficient grounds to do so. I think I quoted enough authorities to show that I was somewhat confused about what I had discovered. If I had found the amendment was out of order it would have been ruled out of order. It was not so ruled because I did not find justification for doing so.

I think you are a marvellous Speaker. I have enjoyed all your decisions.
I pointed out that you were not asked to give a decision. I think you are doing an excellent job.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member should know that I do not have to be asked to give a decision. When I receive an amendment it is my duty to examine it and, without a request from anyone, to make a decision; it is my duty to render one. Had the Prime Minister made no comment at all I was considering the amendment and would have made the comment I have made, in just the same way. That is what I wish to have clear.
The hon. member for Eglinton may proceed.

Mr. Speaker, it is about two minutes to ten. Perhaps we might call it ten o'clock.
